#9713. The Definitive Fine-Tuning Guide for 3D Generation Models

TLDR; In this blog, we provide fine-tuning scripts and containers to fine-tune TRELLIS.2, a popular 3D model on your 3D assets, that can run both locally and on Hugging Face Jobs. If you are interested in fine-tuning, you can use our scripts with few arguments (assuming you updated your dataset to Hugging Face Hub) or tinker with them yourself with this repository. If you want to learn more, we go through how the script works. Let’s go!

3D generation has many uses in robotics, simulation, media, and entertainment. In these fields, it is difficult to make generated objects obey strict rules and standardize model and data representations. There are many file formats, such as GLB and PLY. There are also many representations, such as neural radiance fields (NeRFs) and 3D Gaussian splatting (3DGS). Each one has different advantages and disadvantages.

TRELLIS introduced a common internal representation, called a unified latent representation. Its decoders convert this representation into 3D models in the required output format. Thus, you do not have to use different models for each representation format.

The same team then released TRELLIS.2, which improves the model's representation of 3D structure. But neither model gives an easy way to adapt it to a specific task.

A general-purpose model, such as TRELLIS.2, can make errors in details that are important for a specific application. For example, a user may need accurate geometry for furniture models. Without fine-tuning for that task, the pretrained model can produce geometry that is insufficiently accurate. We use a subset of GSO that has 188 footwear objects for our experiment. In our initial tests, the pretrained model usually produced shoes that looked correct, but the soles were incorrect. We test whether a LoRA can make the soles more accurate.

Our goal is to use the Google Scanned Objects (GSO) dataset to improve the performance of TRELLIS.2 on a specific object category. We will explain which pipeline components to fine-tune and which to leave unchanged during training. The pipeline separates structure, detailed geometry, and materials. Thus, we will fine-tune only the components that are important for our task.

Choosing what to freeze matters as much as choosing what to fine-tune.

LoRA, short for low-rank adaptation, fine-tunes a model by training small adapter matrices while keeping the original weights frozen. This reduces the number of trainable parameters and the memory needed for their gradients and optimizer state. We use Hugging Face’s PEFT library to add and train these adapters. For more information, read our LoRA guide.

Hugging Face Jobs runs containerized workloads on cloud hardware. We use it for preprocessing and for training. To use your own GPU instead, see the local Docker commands below. Before you start, make sure that you have:

Before we train, let’s look at how TRELLIS.2 generates a 3D object and where we’ll add LoRA adapters.

TRELLIS.2 has five main stages: remove the image background, encode the image, predict the coarse structure, generate detailed geometry, and generate materials. The pipeline then exports the result as a textured mesh.

First, BiRefNet removes the background from the input image. DINOv3-L then encodes the image into feature tokens. The generation models use these tokens to guide the 3D object.

The sparse-structure flow DiT predicts the object's coarse shape. It is a diffusion transformer (DiT) that makes a small latent of size 16³ × 8. A variational autoencoder (VAE) decoder then changes this latent into a 64 × 64 × 64 occupancy grid. Each voxel in the grid shows if that location is part of the object. A voxel is a pixel in three dimensions. We add LoRA adapters to this model because its output guides the geometry stage.

O-Voxel is the 3D format of TRELLIS.2. It is a sparse voxel grid. It keeps only the voxels on the object's surface. Each voxel keeps local geometry, such as a mesh vertex, and material attributes. Because the format is small, a CPU changes a mesh into O-Voxel in seconds. A GPU changes O-Voxel back into a mesh in seconds.

Structured sparse latents come from TRELLIS. They keep 3D data in sparse tensors, which makes computation faster. The model uses only approximately 10% of the voxels in the grid, so it does not spend compute on empty voxels. Thus, the shape flow DiT and the texture flow DiT are sparse transformers. The sparse-structure flow DiT is a dense transformer.

The shape flow DiT uses the occupancy grid and the DINOv3 feature tokens to make a latent. Another VAE decoder then changes this latent into O-Voxel geometry at a resolution of 512 × 512 × 512.

We add LoRA adapters to the DiT at this stage because it controls the object's shape.

In the last stage, the texture flow DiT uses the shape latent and the DINOv3 features as input. It defines the materials and textures of the geometry's surface. A VAE decoder then changes the latent into base color, metallic, roughness, and alpha values for each voxel. We do not add LoRA adapters to this stage. Our dataset has diffuse color maps, but it lacks the separate material maps this stage needs for training. Also, our problem is the shoe's shape. The base model already makes good colors and textures.

Finally, the pipeline combines the geometry and material attributes into a textured mesh and exports it as a GLB file.

We add LoRA adapters only to the sparse-structure flow DiT and the shape flow DiT. These DiTs control the object's shape and geometry. We freeze the texture flow DiT to keep its current capabilities.

Our dataset contains diffuse color maps that include baked lighting effects. To train the texture flow DiT, we need separate material maps. The color maps in our dataset mix surface color with lighting. Thus, they are not correct targets for this training.

If we train the texture flow DiT on these maps, it can learn to show lighting as a surface property. It can also forget what it learned before, a problem called catastrophic forgetting.

Our subset has 188 shoes from the 1,030 objects in GSO. For a dataset this small, LoRA is a better choice than full fine-tuning. Full fine-tuning costs much more. It can also overwrite what the model already does well (its learned priors). Our configuration trains approximately 9.3 million adapter parameters in total for both targeted DiTs. We use rank 8 adapters in the attention and feed-forward (MLP) layers of the sparse-structure flow DiT. We use rank 16 adapters in the attention layers of the shape flow DiT. The rank sets the size of the adapter matrices. A higher rank lets the adapter learn more.

A 3D model setup can need many dependencies and installation steps. We supply two Docker images (that you can run on Jobs or your own machine) with the necessary software. One image is for preprocessing, and one is for fine-tuning.

To train your LoRA adapters and upload them to the Hub:

Then we explain the fine-tuning script, its settings, and how each setting affects training.

We’ll walk through three parts of the experiment:

We save the preprocessed dataset so that all training runs can reuse it.

The preprocessing container uses Blender to render 16 views of each object. LoRA training will use these views as conditioning images. Blender runs without a display, through the xvfb-run utility. The container also processes each object through the preprocessing pipeline. See the footwear dataset here for an example intermediate output. For our 188 objects, the full run took approximately 1 hour on an a100-large job. A compact version of the preprocessing pipeline is also available in this companion repository.

For Hugging Face Jobs, we pass the following arguments:

This container accepts a few more arguments (regardless of being run on Hugging Face Jobs or with Docker), that you can find documented over here. The steps taken in the preprocessing pipeline are documented in this section later.

The training container loads the prepared dataset and a configuration preset or file. It records training metrics with Trackio. Use the Trackio dashboard to monitor the run.

We use ‘ss’ and ‘shape’ to indicate the two modes we have for training the LoRAs. The ‘ss’ mode will finetune only the Sparse-Structure Flow DiT, whereas the ‘shape’ mode will finetune the Shape Flow DiT. Under the hood, they simply reference different config.json files to use for each stage. More details about the process is available in this section later.

If you set --push-to, the container uploads adapter checkpoints to the Hub. The container accepts parameters that are also documented here for brevity. A compact script is also available in the same repository.

If you want to play around and fine-tune with the already-processed dataset we have, feel free to use the following set of commands.

The commands and flags are the same as for Hugging Face Jobs. Only the Docker options are different.

If you want to use our already-preprocessed dataset locally on your machine of choice, use the following commands:

Our trained LoRA adapters are in this repository: suvadityamuk/trellis-2-finetune-gso

We use TRELLIS.2’s frozen encoders to convert the input meshes into training latents. We save these latents, so later runs do not have to encode the meshes again.

We also render 16 views of each object in Blender. During training, we select one random view for each sample as the conditioning image. We keep 9 of the 188 objects for evaluation and train on the other 179. These held-out objects show whether the adapters work on objects unseen by the model during training.

Some of the views that Blender rendered for one object

The first snippet sets up the data. FLOW selects the flow DiT to train (ss or shape), and STEPS sets the number of optimizer steps. A batch size of 4 with 4 gradient accumulation steps gives an effective batch size of 16. Then, the snippet loads the LoRA config file for the selected flow DiT, makes the dataset in the TRELLIS.2 format, removes the held-out objects, and makes the data loader for fine-tuning.

We use the peft library to insert LoRA adapters into the selected layers. TRELLIS.2 has a custom forward pass, so the standard PeftModel() wrapper does not work. Instead, we call inject_adapter_in_model(). This function adds the adapters directly to the model and keeps its custom interface.

We keep the trainable adapter weights in 32-bit floating point (fp32) for numerical stability and use bfloat16 (bf16) autocasting for the forward pass. Autocasting lets PyTorch use lower precision for some operations, which decreases memory use. Autocasting does not change how the frozen backbone weights are stored.

It’s important to note that our objective function here is good-old rectified flow matching (as seen in popular image-generation models like Stable Diffusion 3, Flux 2, and others). TRELLIS.2 used the same objective in pretraining, so it is a good choice for fine-tuning. For the theory, read this blog about flow matching.

We update only the LoRA parameters in the sparse-structure and shape DiTs. All original model weights remain frozen.

The snippets below show the core training loop for one stage. They are simpler than the container code and do not include some setup steps. For the full workflow, use the container commands.

We initialize the optimizer and load DINOv3 to extract features from the input images.

We then follow these steps within the training loop:

The training loop computes the loss and updates the adapter weights. Gradient accumulation adds the gradients from 4 small batches before each optimizer step. Gradient checkpointing saves GPU memory by recomputing some intermediate values during backpropagation. The outer loop runs for a given number of optimizer steps, whereas the inner loop accumulates gradients over a set of batches.

For each batch, DINOv3 encodes the conditioning image. For classifier-free guidance (CFG) dropout, the loop sets the conditioning to zero for a random fraction (p_uncond) of the samples. Then, it calculates the flow-matching loss with bf16 autocasting. After the inner loop, it clips the gradients to prevent very large updates and does an optimizer step. It logs the loss every 10 steps and saves an adapter checkpoint every 500 steps.

We trained two adapters: one for the sparse-structure DiT and one for the shape DiT. The LoRA config files in the container image contain the full training settings: ss_flow_lora_gso.json for the sparse-structure flow DiT and slat_flow_img2shape_lora_gso.json for the shape flow DiT. Each run used one A100 80 GB on Hugging Face Jobs. The sparse-structure run took 7.2 hours, and the shape run took 3.6 hours.

The training loss of the sparse-structure flow DiT falls quickly at the start, then more slowly. The loss of the shape flow DiT stays at approximately the same level. These curves show how the training objective changes, but they do not directly measure the quality of the generated geometry.

Flow-matching loss varies with the sampled objects, noise, and timesteps. To find out if fine-tuning improves the geometry, we must also compare outputs on the held-out objects.

The figure below compares outputs for five of the nine held-out objects. It shows the input image, the base model’s generated output, the base output after a rotation adjustment, the output with the footwear adapters, and the reference scan. In these examples, the soles from the fine-tuned model are closer to the scans.

We also use three metrics to evaluate the geometry on the test set:

In the chart’s nine-object comparison, the base model has a mean F-score of 0.276, compared with 0.803 for the model with the footwear adapters. Chamfer distance falls from 0.174 to 0.033, and normal consistency rises from 0.530 to 0.804. With both adapters, the F-score is better on all nine held-out objects.

For the statistics of all runs, see this Trackio space.

Phew, so there we go! We fine-tuned TRELLIS.2 for footwear generation by adding LoRA adapters to the two model components that control geometry. We prepared the data once, trained the adapters in separate jobs, and evaluated the outputs on held-out objects.

The main lesson is to select a training target that agrees with the problem and the data that you have. For this experiment, we fine-tuned the structure and shape stages and froze the texture stage.

Next, we can examine if the same choices help other 3D generation models, such as Pixal3D and UniLat3D.

Gaussian-splat and world-generation models, such as HunyuanWorld 2.0 and NVIDIA Lyra 2.0, are also possible next steps. Their representations and training pipelines can need different methods.

Thank you for following along, and see you in the next one! 👋🤗

#9711. ProWritingAid VS Grammarly: Which Grammar Checker is Better in (2022) ?

Grammarly is a tool that checks for grammatical errors, spelling, and punctuation.it gives you comprehensive feedback on your writing. You can use this tool to proofread and edit articles, blog posts, emails, etc.

Grammarly also detects all types of mistakes, including sentence structure issues and misused words. It also gives you suggestions on style changes, punctuation, spelling, and grammar all are in real-time. The free version covers the basics like identifying grammar and spelling mistakes

whereas the Premium version offers a lot more functionality, it detects plagiarism in your content, suggests word choice, or adds fluency to it.

ProWritingAid is a style and grammar checker for content creators and writers. It helps to optimize word choice, punctuation errors, and common grammar mistakes, providing detailed reports to help you improve your writing.

ProWritingAid can be used as an add-on to WordPress, Gmail, and Google Docs. The software also offers helpful articles, videos, quizzes, and explanations to help improve your writing.

Here are some key features of ProWriting Aid:

Grammarly and ProWritingAid are well-known grammar-checking software. However, if you're like most people who can't decide which to use, here are some different points that may be helpful in your decision.

As both writing assistants are great in their own way, you need to choose the one that suits you best.

Both ProWritingAid and Grammarly are awesome writing tools, without a doubt. but as per my experience, Grammarly is a winner here because Grammarly helps you to review and edit your content. Grammarly highlights all the mistakes in your writing within seconds of copying and pasting the content into Grammarly’s editor or using the software’s native feature in other text editors.

Not only does it identify tiny grammatical and spelling errors, it tells you when you overlook punctuations where they are needed. And, beyond its plagiarism-checking capabilities, Grammarly helps you proofread your content. Even better, the software offers a free plan that gives you access to some of its features.

I use the paid versions of both Grammarly and Pro Writing Aid. Both of them have issues:- Grammarly IS more focused on nonfiction than fiction. If you're writing fiction, you may find Grammarly's insistence on "Conciseness" annoying. They seem to want to take the soul out of your writing, which is fine for a corporate report or technical manual, but not for your Great American Novel.- Grammarly pushes features on users that are not ready for prime time. It doesn't matter that you never agreed to be a beta tester for them; you get to do it anyway.- Pro Writing Aid actually counts the occurrences of words in your document and tells you when a word has been overused compared to published literature. Grammarly, on the other hand, seems hell-bent to remove certain words that it has deemed overused from the language, whether or not they're actually overused in your document.- Grammarly's Clarity function is simply horrible. It mangles sentences and changes their meaning. Sometimes the result of its suggestion is unintelligible garbage.- Grammarly allows you to turn off some checks, but not all of them. Unfortunately, the ones you cannot turn off are some of the most irritating (such as that horrible "Clarity"). On the other hand, Pro Writing Aid lets you choose which checks you use.- Pro Writing Aid has a mediocre command of American English (it's a British product). The app insists on rules of grammar and spelling that are outright wrong, per Merriam-Webster, the Chicago Manual of Style, and modern usage as shown by Google Books Ngram. At one point, Pro Writing Aid insisted that American English did not include the words "holiday" and "autumn," that "vacation" and "fall" must be used instead.- Pro Writing Aid's rules for commas are 100 percent consistent with the way I learned them in high school--50 years ago! They do not reflect modern usage. Grammarly is much better at this.- Pro Writing Aid seems to waste their limited resources on tweaking their UI. Their UI most definitely could use improvement, but these changes are not great improvements; they only serve to confuse users. Their resources would be better spent fixing the many functional problems in their app.- Some of Pro Writing Aid's checks are completely useless, as they do not take context into consideration. For example, an ordinary word would not be capitalized as part of a narrative, but would be as part of a title (for example, "professor." But if you capitalize correctly for context, Pro Writing Aid dings you for "Inconsistent capitalization." Similar issues exist with hyphenation consistency check.Each of these applications has its strengths as well as considerable weaknesses. I will say that both of them are light-years better than the execrable grammar checker in Microsoft Word, but that's damning with faint praise.

#9710. One Abuse Complaint Later: Hardening a Home Proxy Without Blocking All UDP

Systems & Mobile Engineer, 18+ years. Linux and Android internals, iOS, embedded firmware, and stories from the debugging bench.

Systems & Mobile Engineer, 18+ years. Linux and Android internals, iOS, embedded firmware, and stories from the debugging bench.

Systems & Mobile Engineer, 18+ years. Linux and Android internals, iOS, embedded firmware, and stories from the debugging bench.

This piece continues a previous write-up on diagnosing injected TCP resets [1]. That one was about proving where a connection failed. This one is about keeping a shared exit within its provider's rules and recoverable when its own tooling fails.

The setup is boring on purpose. One cheap virtual server, a gigabit port, a proxy core (Xray) with a REALITY inbound, and a house full of devices that route through it by domain rules on the router. Nothing exotic; the build takes an evening and about twenty dollars a year. It served video, cloud sync, and late night music discovery before this incident.

Then a family member installed a torrent client.

The client did what torrent clients do. It announced itself to public trackers, joined the public DHT network through its bootstrap nodes, and started moving gigabytes at line rate. Nobody in the house noticed anything; the video streams were fine, the ping was fine, everything was fine.

Forty minutes later the hoster forwarded the first abuse complaint. The message was professionally assembled: a timestamp with a timezone, the exact protocol their sensor had matched, both endpoints of the observed flow, and a link to the acceptable use policy. The complaint documented a flow associated with the exit address. I could not reconstruct the monitoring system behind it from that notice alone.

The policy page left no room for creativity. Repeat complaints end with the address null-routed, and null-routed budget servers do not get appeal processes. The exit had to become hostile to BitTorrent, and it had to happen before the next evening, because torrent clients tend to run on schedules. Whoever starts the client, the operator of the exit answers for what leaves it.

The instinctive fix, and I almost shipped it, reads one line long: block UDP. The reasoning is sound as far as it goes. The DHT and uTP use UDP, so blocking UDP removes important paths. It does not stop TCP peer connections or every tracker.

In my incident, observed torrent traffic stopped. Several unrelated applications broke too.

The first attempt dropped every UDP flow on the exit except DNS on port 53. Torrent traffic stopped within minutes, which looked like victory for about an hour.

Messenger calls were disrupted while text messages continued to work. WhatsApp survived through TCP fallback. Blocking UDP did not make every call impossible; it made the household depend on whichever fallback each application could manage.

The split between messages and calls was the useful clue. A service could remain reachable while one of its communication paths was blocked. I removed the blanket rule and tested calls again.

QUIC was affected too. I did not measure a browser-wide latency penalty. Games and browser videoconferencing belong in the regression checklist; I did not keep controlled results for them.

That is the trap with a transport-level block: ordinary browsing and messaging can make the connection look healthy while other functions fail. A dashboard of established TCP sessions would not establish that UDP-dependent traffic still worked.

The lesson cost one evening. Blocking an entire transport was too broad for accidental BitTorrent use on this shared exit. The replacement needed narrower rules and tests of the household applications that mattered.

A client needs a way to discover peers before it can transfer data. Common starting points include trackers, DHT bootstrap nodes, and information already stored locally.

These sources overlap, but they are not a closed list. Trackers may use hostnames or IP addresses. Clients can retain peers and DHT routing tables across restarts. Torrent files may contain node addresses, and users can supply peers directly.

BEP 5 explicitly describes persistent routing tables and embedded nodes. A hostname deny list cannot remove that knowledge from a client.

The objective here is narrower: reduce the discovery paths available to ordinary household clients, while avoiding a blanket UDP block. This is a mitigation for accidental use, not a guarantee against another complaint. Where the hoster's policy requires reliable prevention, endpoint controls or keeping untrusted devices off the shared exit remain necessary.

Translated into ordered routing rules on the exit node:

Four checks are expressed as three routing rules: the protocol sniffer, tracker list, bootstrap names, and port range. The tracker list and bootstrap names share one domain rule.

These rules have two prerequisites. Enable traffic sniffing on every inbound that carries the traffic being filtered, and provide the block outbound. Merge this field into each existing inbound, keeping its listener, credentials, and transport settings:

Add this object to the existing outbounds array if the tag is not already defined:

The snippets are configuration fragments, not a replacement configuration. Keep the ordinary outbound first: it remains the default for unmatched traffic. Without enabled payload sniffing, the BitTorrent protocol rule cannot identify its handshake. bittorrent is not a destOverride value; that list controls supported hostname overrides. Here, routeOnly: true uses the sniffed hostname for routing without replacing the connection's destination address. If the inbound already has a sniffing policy, reconcile it rather than replacing it blindly.

The protocol sniffer catches plain BitTorrent handshakes on any port. Honesty matters here, and the documentation is refreshingly blunt about it: the built-in sniffer is basic and may miss encrypted or obfuscated handshakes. Treat it as a tripwire, not a wall. Its usefulness depends on the handshake that actually reaches the sniffer.

The tracker list is a community-maintained geosite category. Its coverage changes, so verify the domains relevant to your clients instead of assuming it includes every default tracker.

The four DHT names in the rule above are useful bootstrap targets to cover, not a universal or mandatory bootstrap set. Other names, direct addresses, saved routing tables, and embedded nodes can bypass them.

A domain rule needs a domain to match. DNS resolution on a laptop does not automatically reveal that name to the exit server. What matters is what the proxy receives or can recover.

A proxy destination containing a hostname

Confirm the client actually sends the hostname

An IP destination with a supported name-bearing handshake

Inspect the configured sniffer and routing behavior

The packet need not contain the bootstrap name

A cached peer or manually entered address

That distinction explains a frustrating test result: the list can contain the right hostname while the connection still passes. Adding more names will not fix missing name visibility.

The installer below is idempotent. It cleans its tagged rules before writing replacements, including the blanket-UDP attempt from Part 2. Re-running it does not duplicate its tagged rules. The marker uses Xray's documented ruleTag field. Review the two legacy shapes before using it: exact equality cannot prove who originally created a rule. The installer assumes the inbound sniffing settings and block outbound are already configured.

Run the installer with permission to preserve the original file's owner and group. My service reads a root:xray configuration with mode 0640. Copying only that mode to a root-created temporary file can leave it owned by root:root, making the replacement unreadable to the service. The snippet preserves ownership before replacement and creates the temporary file privately. A successful validation as root does not prove that the service account can read it; check the configuration under the actual service user before restarting.

Testing covered three properties, because duplicates are not the only way to fail. A double run produced no duplicated rules, because cleanup now keys on the ruleTag and cannot miss its own output. A scratch config carrying a foreign UDP rule and a foreign bittorrent-shaped rule kept both untouched: only tagged rules and the two known pre-tag shapes are removed. The write path goes through a backup, a temporary file, an Xray configuration test, and an atomic replace. The code writes the file; applying it to the running service is a separate step. An earlier version matched every UDP rule as removable, and the one after it read one field while writing another, creating a duplicate per run. Both mistakes stay in this paragraph as a warning: installers are code, and code needs tests.

One more bug survived the test doubles. Xray infers the configuration format from the filename unless told otherwise; config.json.tmp has an unsupported extension. My stub returned success without checking that. On Xray 26.3.27 for macOS arm64, the old installer failed with "Failed to get format" and left the original file untouched. The correction explicitly selects JSON. The final snippet, including mkstemp and ownership preservation, then passed two runs as root with real Xray 26.3.27 for Linux arm64 in a disposable container. Both runs preserved foreign rules and root:xray ownership with mode 0640; validation also passed as the xray user. An invalid configuration was rejected without replacing the original or leaving a temporary file. These checks exercise configuration loading and file access, not live traffic filtering.

Choose a tracker URL that answers through the unfiltered route. Use its real protocol; an HTTPS request to a UDP-only tracker is not a useful control.

A timeout or TLS failure alone does not identify the blocking component. Compare the same endpoint with the relevant rule disabled, then enabled, and correlate the result with routing logs. Run a reachable control request too. Do this in a controlled test window, using authorized content and a test device.

The following matrix makes the boundary visible before trusting the policy:

Fresh client, selected tracker and bootstrap paths

A rule match and failed discovery on those paths

Same client with retained peers or DHT state

Whether transfers resume despite hostname filters

Call or QUIC session through the same exit

Every application or UDP port is unaffected

Hostname filtering can see raw IP traffic

Record the Xray version, client version, rule order, and whether the client state was fresh. A screenshot of an idle torrent client omits all four.

Do not pipe curl into head and treat the pipeline status as curl's result. Without pipefail, a successful final command can hide an earlier failure. Capture the status of the command being tested directly.

Four other designs got considered and rejected before the layered approach, and the reasons are instructive.

Blocking torrents on the router by DNS failed for two reasons. First, devices with hardcoded DNS or DNS-over-HTTPS bypass the router resolver entirely, and the exit cannot assume every device uses its resolver. Second, DNS filtering says nothing about direct IP connections, and DHT speaks raw UDP to addresses.

Per-device policing, the management answer, does not survive contact with guests and phones. It also pushes the problem onto people who cannot debug it, which converts an engineering task into a series of arguments.

Port-based blocking alone, without the domain layers, fails because modern clients randomize their listening ports on first run. The 6881-6889 range stays in the rule set anyway, as a cheap belt under the suspenders, but nothing depends on it.

Rate limiting torrent-shaped traffic was the most tempting sophisticated option and the easiest to reject. Shaping requires classifying the flow, which returns to the encrypted-handshake problem, and slower traffic can still participate in a monitored swarm. Lower transfer speed does not eliminate the risk of an abuse complaint.

Some client networks, mostly mobile, drop long-lived connections. On those paths the TCP profile sometimes failed in a recognizable pattern: a TLS handshake error, then timeouts, while ICMP still answered. A second inbound using the XHTTP transport in stream-one mode, on the same routing table, worked where the TCP profile failed in my tests. I did not determine why the paths behaved differently; the second inbound is a comparison path, not a diagnosis.

The full transport story, including the sniffing trap that silently disables domain rules when clients resolve locally, belongs in its own write-up. Two details travel with this article because they cost an hour each: in this tested configuration, Vision belongs on the TCP profile; the XHTTP profile omits that flow flag. Sniffing can recover supported names when a client sends an IP destination. Connections already addressed by hostname do not need sniffing for that name to be available.

A later experiment with an additional TLS endpoint exposed another test boundary. Server-side checks passed: the publicly trusted certificate validated, and the listener accepted requests. From the household client, traffic still stalled; an independent client reproduced the failure. The same request sent through an SSH forward to the same listener completed. That comparison placed the failure on the direct network path rather than in the server configuration, without identifying its cause. I removed the experimental endpoint. A server-side smoke test had never proved that the household could use it.

A defense built on domain lists is only as fresh as the lists, so the exit needs a geo database update job. This section exists because mine failed in the most educational way possible.

An installer download returned HTML instead of shell source. My preserved setup guide used the form bash -c "$(curl ...)": command substitution puts the response into a single command-line argument. A large response can exceed the operating system's argument limit before Bash parses any of it. That is consistent with the recorded "Argument list too long" failure. Piping a response into Bash's standard input is a different mechanism; it does not hit that argument-size limit.

The recovery lesson was to stop treating a downloaded response as executable source before checking it. The smaller updater below fetches only data files, validates the configuration that uses them, and attempts to restore the old files if replacement fails.

The following Linux example updates databases only. It does not update the Xray binary or systemd unit. It assumes both old database files exist and runs with permission to replace them and restart Xray. It requires flock, supplied by util-linux on Ubuntu.

The lock is acquired before downloads, backups, or replacements. A competing invocation exits without touching the shared backup files. Every updater that writes these databases must use the same lock path. The shell keeps file descriptor 9 open through recovery and releases the lock on exit; keep the lock file in place rather than deleting it. A different updater that ignores this lock can still race with the example.

In the Linux container test, a held lock rejected a competing invocation before any download, backup, or service command. With the lock free, the updater completed and released it on exit. The test used real flock and Xray validation; downloads and service-control commands were test doubles.

An active process is the first health check, not the last. Confirm every expected listener with ss -lntp, using the ports in your configuration. Then send a control request through the actual client profile. A local request on the VPS bypasses the inbound and cannot substitute for that test. These checks remain separate from the small database-update script.

The -f flag makes curl fail on HTTP errors, explicit failure branches cover the mutation steps; set -e provides additional exit behavior with shell-specific exceptions, the size floors catch truncation, and the first-byte check rejects a leading <. It misses HTML with leading whitespace and many other invalid payloads. None of that proves the database is valid, so the pipeline ends by asking Xray itself: config validation, restart, health check, and a rollback to the saved copies if any step objects. The updater attempts to restore the previous databases and restart Xray. Both restore copies are attempted, and backups are retained. An incomplete restore stops before restart and reports that manual intervention is required. Claiming more than that would be selling the guards past what they do.

The meta-lesson generalizes past geo databases: an update pipeline is a threat surface against your own infrastructure, and it deserves the same paranoia as a public endpoint.

The original failure taught me to test the updater's recovery path separately from a normal update. Replacing curl, systemctl, and the installer with test doubles lets a local harness force failures without changing a server.

There are three separate questions. Did the script exit with failure? Did it restore the previous files? Can the service start with those files? A passing answer to the first says nothing about the other two.

For the database-only example, inject a failure into each install, configuration validation, restart, and the active-state check. Compare restored file contents with the saved originals. Also fail each restore copy independently. Verify that both copies are attempted and the backups remain. Fail recovery validation and restart separately; each must report failure without claiming recovery.

A full binary updater needs more tests. Preserve executable permissions, unit files, and the previous presence or absence of installer-created paths. A backup command returning success is not enough; verify that the expected backup exists and contains the original data.

These are suggested release checks, not claims that a stubbed service models a live kernel. A local harness can prove script branches and file restoration. It cannot prove that an upstream archive, service manager, or network behaves exactly like the stub.

Test the snippets extracted from the article itself. A passing test of a different working copy does not verify what the reader will run.

Correct routing rules were not the end of hardening this exit. A later slowdown exposed a different limit: Linux was under TCP memory pressure while hundreds of megabytes of system RAM remained available.

Selected destinations then used a separate process: Xray forwarded them to warp-svc through a loopback SOCKS listener. An October 27 audit of WARP 2026.8.2115.0 found 33 socket descriptors in TCP_CLOSE holding 115.26 MiB, plus six sockets in FIN_WAIT2 holding another 28.59 MiB. Global TCP memory was 144.72 MiB. Two snapshots thirty seconds apart showed the same allocations; some half-closed connections had retained data for over forty minutes.

TCP_CLOSE described the protocol state. The process still held descriptors referring to those sockets, and their buffers remained charged. The initial ss output did not account for all of it. Following the process's descriptors, duplicating them with pidfd_getfd, and querying SO_MEMINFO and TCP_INFO found the missing allocations. The audit did not read payloads or close the original descriptors.

Restarting only WARP, without changing Xray or its configuration, reduced global TCP memory from 144.72 to 6.11 MiB. A new half-closed WARP socket soon retained about 5 MiB again. The restart identified the process holding the buffers; it did not establish the internal defect or eliminate its cause. Nor was tcp_fin_timeout a general cleanup switch: the Linux documentation defines it for orphaned FIN_WAIT_2 connections, whereas this socket still had an application reference.

A bounded reproduction bypassed Xray and used WARP's SOCKS listener directly. It mixed completed uploads, cancelled downloads, and uploads whose destination replied before consuming the body. Early-response cases retained buffers thirty seconds after completion in two of three runs. The third retained none at that checkpoint. All three actually used H3, even when warp-cli displayed an H2 setting. Requesting a transport had not proved it was in use.

An isolated replacement test used Xray 26.10.21's native MASQUE outbound with verified H2. After six rounds totaling thirty requests, the test instance's cgroup memory fell to 9.93 MiB two minutes after the workload ended. Implementation and device registration changed too, so this was not a controlled H2-versus-H3 comparison.

After migration, the old loopback hop was gone. Absence of its sockets could not prove that the replacement released its own buffers: native MASQUE uses a userspace network stack. Roughly forty-six hours later, the production Xray instance's cgroup held 25.08 MiB, including 23.45 MiB of anonymous memory, with a peak of 187.01 MiB of unknown timing and cause. That cgroup peak and the old kernel socket allocation measure different things. Four additional TCP-pressure episodes totaled about 6.6 seconds; their cause was also unknown. The snapshot showed memory had fallen, not permanent leak elimination.

A successful response establishes delivery. Hardening also means checking what remains allocated after completion, cancellation, and an early response. Otherwise, a correct traffic policy can still leave the next evening's allowed traffic competing for resources held by finished requests.

Scope: this article covers running a personal proxy within a hosting provider's acceptable use policy. Check your provider's terms and the laws that apply where you and your users are before operating one.

#9709. [AI in Action] First Time Using Herdr: Collaborating with Claude Code and agy for Go Backend Code Review, Issue Fixes, and Cloud

Posted on Nov 12 • Originally published at evanlin.com on Nov 12

song-lingo is a small tool I made for learning Japanese songs: paste a YouTube MV link, and Gemini helps me transcribe the lyrics, label Romanization (Romaji), provide Traditional Chinese translation and grammar notes, and then uses Gemini TTS to generate a "teacher demonstration audio." After I record myself shadowing the song, Gemini transcribes my pronunciation and provides a word-by-word score.

A few days ago, in a single Claude Code session, I rewrote the entire backend from Python + Next.js API routes to Go 1.26 (Issues #44–#49, Tracking Issue #50, PR #51–#56). The architecture after the rewrite looks like this:

The rewrite was done, it worked, and tests passed. But "writing and reviewing your own code" always has blind spots. I happened to want to try Herdr—a tool that allows multiple AI Agents to collaborate in the same window, each occupying a Pane. So, I conducted an experiment:

Let Claude Code be the controller and Reviewer on the left, and the Antigravity CLI (agy) be the implementer on the right. The two Agents communicate via Herdr, taking the song-lingo Go backend from Code Review all the way to Cloud Run deployment.

A small side note: I initially told Claude Code to "use herdr --skill to learn first," but the herdr command couldn't be found—the actual executables are ~/.local/bin/herdr-app and ~/.local/bin/herdr-core.

I think Herdr's smartest design is that both CLIs have a --skill parameter. Running herdr-app --skill and herdr-core --skill prints an "instruction manual for AI Agents."

So, Claude Code's first step wasn't to blindly try commands, but to read both manuals before starting. The manuals contain many sensible guidelines, such as: background Agents must use --bg, provide a name and clear scope, don't let sub-agents spawn more sub-agents, and use hc wait instead of sleep polling when waiting.

This is the most critical piece of the collaboration. When assigning a task, I would require agy: "When finished, please run herdr-core send t4 '...' to report back." After agy finishes, that message appears directly in Claude Code's input, looking like this:

In other words, Claude Code doesn't need to keep staring at the right screen; agy will "knock on the door" when done. Reporting is asynchronous, and every message carries a source address for tracking.

The first time I had Claude Code open agy, it used hc run --bg to run it in the background—it worked functionally, but I couldn't see what agy was doing. So, the second time, I specifically requested "in a pane on the right," and Claude Code used herdr-app do pane.split to open agy on the right. The final configuration was:

The first task was simple: ask agy to review the Go code under backend/, read-only, no subagents, and write the results to a file, reporting back with hc send t4 when finished.

agy's interface showed it was running Claude Sonnet 5.5 (plan mode), and it eventually produced 17 issues, sorted by importance. Claude Code helped me organize them into three categories:

Here is a detail I really liked: Claude Code did not accept everything blindly. Before opening an Issue, it first used grep to verify the most important one—"re-annotate and review use different mutexes"—and only after confirming it was true did it start opening Issues. The Reviewer's conclusions also need to be Reviewed.

"Open issues and fix them sequentially. Mainly let the agy pane on the right do the modifications. You are responsible for reviewing and giving feedback. Only after you approve should agy commit and push."

Claude Code consolidated the 17 items into 5 Issues (#57–#61), all performed on the same branch go-review-fixes, with one commit per Issue, and commit messages including Fixes #N.

This is the part I want to share the most. Out of the 5 Issues, 3 required a second round of fixes, and 2 passed on the first try:

agy's per-song lock design was correct. Claude Code also specifically confirmed one thing: manual translations and the reviewed flag are both written into the transcript, so "comparing the entire transcript before writing back" indeed catches all edits.

But agy didn't write tests. So Claude Code requested extracting the logic into saveAnnotation and adding two cases: normal write when unchanged, and return conflict and no write when edited.

While cleaning up the failure cache, agy deleted the server-side recentErrors. All tests passed, but Claude Code caught a regression:

When the TTS quota is exhausted, "other sentences that have never been generated" checking ?error would get {error: null}—the frontend then couldn't display the reason "quota exhausted."

The fix was to make LastError return a still-valid quota error when there is no failure record for that sentence, and add a test.

This was the most valuable bug catch in my opinion. The graceful shutdown agy wrote was: srv.Shutdown waits 10s, then background jobs wait another 10s. There were two problems:

Claude Code requested changing it to a single 9-second deadline and adjusting the sequence:

(The above is illustrative of the sequence and single-deadline concept.)

Looking back at these three rejected Issues, there's a common theme: they were all "tests pass, but it hurts in production" problems—test gaps, frontend error message regressions, and shutdown sequences. This is exactly the greatest value of "one writing, one reviewing."

After all 5 commits passed, PR #62 was opened and merged, and #57–#61 were automatically closed. Then, a new revision was deployed using gcloud run deploy --source ..

Post-deployment verification was completed by Claude Code running fetch directly through a Chrome instance logged into IAP:

The previous revision was also kept, allowing for an immediate rollback if needed.

Intuitively, you might start agy like this:

The result is an immediate error and exit (exit 2):

The correct way is agy -i "..."—interactive startup with an initial task. The Herdr manual also warns not to use -p one-off mode, because the Agent needs to remain "observable and follow-upable" to conduct the Review back-and-forth.

The first time you start agy in a folder, it pops up "Do you trust the contents of this project?". At this point, the hc get status becomes blocked (auth). Claude Code just needs to use hc keys go-review enter to confirm.

After opening agy with pane.split, the screen looks idle, and the initial prompt seems unsent. Claude Code tried to resend it with hc send, but was blocked by hc:

It turns out the task had already arrived, and agy was just stuck waiting for permission. This protection mechanism in hc prevents accidentally typing a task description into a permission dialog—if that actually happened, the result could be an unintended approval or rejection of a command.

When agy is in plan mode (read-only research), it can only analyze. To have it start modifying code, you must press shift+tab to switch modes; Claude Code used hc keys t7 shift+tab to switch it. The first round of Code Review was perfect for plan mode, and it only switched out when modifications were needed in the second round.

Every shell command in agy requires permission. Pressing Enter for each one is too tedious, so Claude Code wrote a small driver script with the following logic:

This script was refined several times during the process, each time providing a practical lesson:

The line for automated granting was drawn like this:

Agents can trust each other enough to say "you can run tests," but "writing to git, writing to the cloud, making external requests" must go through a Reviewer or a human.

If you also want to use Herdr (or similar tools) to have two Agents write and review, you can refer to this checklist:

As I finish writing this, agy on the right is already running the next task: using its GCP skill to analyze song-lingo's performance on Cloud Run—service settings, cold starts, gcsfuse, Firestore, etc.—proposing 5–8 solutions, each with evidence, expected benefits, monthly costs, and risks, for Claude Code to decide which to implement. This part is still ongoing; I'll share more later.

My biggest takeaway from using Herdr for the first time is: Multi-Agent collaboration is finally "visible."

And this article itself was written by Claude Code in the rightmost Pane of Herdr—after finishing, it will use herdr-core send t4 to report back to the controller on the left.

#9706. It Worked Locally… But Did It Match Staging? Meet DiffLens

Posted on Nov 12 • Edited on Nov 12 • AI-assisted

Have you ever finished a UI change, opened staging, and wondered: “What exactly changed between my local build and staging?”

A manual check can miss small layout shifts, changed text, or unexpected DOM updates. I built DiffLens to make those differences easier to inspect.

DiffLens is a local web app that compares a local page against a staging page in three independent ways:

DiffLens — Compare. Understand. Ship with confidence.

A screenshot comparison is useful, but it only answers part of the question.

These are different kinds of changes, so DiffLens treats them as separate comparison layers.

DiffLens captures both pages using Chromium at a fixed 1920 × 1080 viewport, then compares the screenshots using pixelmatch.

Changed pixels are highlighted over a faded local screenshot. The UI provides side-by-side, slider-overlay, and diff-only views.

The comparison summary also reports the percentage of pixels that differ. Treat this as a signal for investigation rather than a pass/fail score: dynamic content, font rendering, and page movement can all affect the result.

The content layer compares visible page text (innerText) line by line using the diff library. Adjacent delete/add pairs are presented as word-level modifications.

Staging is the baseline; local is the candidate:

The markup layer compares element snapshots matched by rendered CSS path. It reports new nodes, removed nodes, text changes, and tracked attribute changes such as href, src, alt, aria-*, and form attributes.

Before capture, DiffLens blocks service workers, freezes animations and transitions, waits for fonts and images, and scrolls the page to trigger lazy-loaded content. It captures visible text, element snapshots, console/network diagnostics, and screenshots.

The three diff layers then run and their results are assembled into a report.

Both pages use the same capture settings:

DiffLens uses Chromium because visual comparison requires actual layout and paint. The Chromium build is installed for Playwright. pixelmatch powers screenshot comparison, while the diff library handles text comparison. Markup comparison uses captured element snapshots.

The visual layer compares the two captured screenshots and identifies changed pixels.

The content layer compares captured visible text, treating staging as the baseline and local as the candidate.

For markup, DiffLens captures each element's CSS path, tag, own text, and tracked attributes. The snapshots are matched by CSS path to identify additions, removals, and updates.

These snippets illustrate the approach; they are not copied from the project's internal modules.

A visual or content difference is easier to investigate when you can also see how each page loaded. DiffLens includes a Diagnostics view with information for both sides, including HTTP status, page title, viewport, page height, visible text size, scanned element count, links/buttons/images, capture time, and console or request errors.

DiffLens supports preemptive Basic Auth on each side independently. Static comparisons pass credentials to Playwright through httpCredentials.

Passwords are not persisted to localStorage, sent to the server, or included in exported artifacts. The UI stores only the username for display, and the password field is cleared after the session ends.

Each comparison produces a self-contained HTML report with embedded screenshots and a JSON result. Screenshots, text snapshots, and result.json are stored under .artifacts//; the latest 40 runs are retained.

Open http://127.0.0.1:4173 and select Try the demo. The bundled demo pages contain intentional differences so you can explore all three comparison layers.

To compare your own pages, enter a local URL such as http://localhost:3000 and a staging URL such as https://staging.example.com. Select Compare pages, or use ⌘ + Enter on macOS / Ctrl + Enter on Windows and Linux.

DiffLens fetches the URLs you provide, including internal hosts. It binds to 127.0.0.1 by default. Do not expose it to an untrusted network without adding authentication and appropriate SSRF protections. Only HTTP and HTTPS URLs are accepted.

The next step for DiffLens is synchronized live rendering. Instead of comparing captured screenshots, this mode will render the local and staging pages side by side in the same workspace, so you can interact with both versions while reviewing them.

This will build on DiffLens's existing comparison workflow by making it easier to inspect not only what changed in a capture, but also how both versions behave during the same interaction.

If you work on frontend applications, QA, or UI testing, give it a try and let me know what would make it more useful.

Compare a local web app against staging and see exactly what changed — visually, in the text, and in the markup.

DiffLens is a local web app for reviewing changes between a local build and a staging environment. It renders both pages in Chromium at the same 1920 × 1080 viewport, then produces three independent comparisons:

Comparison What you get Visual Full-page pixel comparison. Changed pixels are highlighted over a faded local screenshot. Inspect side-by-side, slider-overlay, or diff-only views. Content Visible text compared line by line, with word-level highlights for modified lines. Staging is the baseline; local is the candidate. Markup DOM elements matched by rendered CSS path, including added and removed nodes, text changes, and tracked attribute changes such as href, src, and alt.

Every comparison also produces a self-contained…

If you find it useful, consider starring the repository, opening an issue, or contributing an improvement.

DiffLens — Compare. Understand. Ship with confidence.

#9703. What is Blockchain: Everything You Need to Know (2022)

Imagine a world in which you can do transactions and many other things without having to give your personal information. A world in which you don’t need to rely on banks or governments anymore. Sounds amazing, right? That’s exactly what blockchain technology allows us to do.

It’s like your computer’s hard drive. blockchain is a technology that lets you store data in digital blocks, which are connected together like links in a chain.

Blockchain technology was originally invented in 1991 by two mathematicians, Stuart Haber and W. Scot Stornetta. They first proposed the system to ensure that timestamps could not be tampered with.

A few years later, in 1998, software developer Nick Szabo proposed using a similar kind of technology to secure a digital payments system he called “Bit Gold.” However, this innovation was not adopted until Satoshi Nakamoto claimed to have invented the first Blockchain and Bitcoin.

A blockchain is a distributed database shared between the nodes of a computer network. It saves information in digital format. Many people first heard of blockchain technology when they started to look up information about bitcoin.

Blockchain is used in cryptocurrency systems to ensure secure, decentralized records of transactions.

Blockchain allowed people to guarantee the fidelity and security of a record of data without the need for a third party to ensure accuracy.

To understand how a blockchain works, Consider these basic steps:

Let’s get to know more about the blockchain.

Blockchain records digital information and distributes it across the network without changing it. The information is distributed among many users and stored in an immutable, permanent ledger that can't be changed or destroyed. That's why blockchain is also called "Distributed Ledger Technology" or DLT.

And that’s the beauty of it! The process may seem complicated, but it’s done in minutes with modern technology. And because technology is advancing rapidly, I expect things to move even more quickly than ever.

Even though blockchain is integral to cryptocurrency, it has other applications. For example, blockchain can be used for storing reliable data about transactions. Many people confuse blockchain with cryptocurrencies like bitcoin and ethereum.

Blockchain already being adopted by some big-name companies, such as Walmart, AIG, Siemens, Pfizer, and Unilever. For example, IBM's Food Trust uses blockchain to track food's journey before reaching its final destination.

Although some of you may consider this practice excessive, food suppliers and manufacturers adhere to the policy of tracing their products because bacteria such as E. coli and Salmonella have been found in packaged foods. In addition, there have been isolated cases where dangerous allergens such as peanuts have accidentally been introduced into certain products.

Tracing and identifying the sources of an outbreak is a challenging task that can take months or years. Thanks to the Blockchain, however, companies now know exactly where their food has been—so they can trace its location and prevent future outbreaks.

Blockchain technology allows systems to react much faster in the event of a hazard. It also has many other uses in the modern world.

Blockchain technology is safe, even if it’s public. People can access the technology using an internet connection.

Have you ever been in a situation where you had all your data stored at one place and that one secure place got compromised? Wouldn't it be great if there was a way to prevent your data from leaking out even when the security of your storage systems is compromised?

Blockchain technology provides a way of avoiding this situation by using multiple computers at different locations to store information about transactions. If one computer experiences problems with a transaction, it will not affect the other nodes.

Instead, other nodes will use the correct information to cross-reference your incorrect node. This is called “Decentralization,” meaning all the information is stored in multiple places.

Blockchain guarantees your data's authenticity—not just its accuracy, but also its irreversibility. It can also be used to store data that are difficult to register, like legal contracts, state identifications, or a company's product inventory.

Blockchain has many advantages and disadvantages.

I’ll answer the most frequently asked questions about blockchain in this section.

Blockchain is not a cryptocurrency but a technology that makes cryptocurrencies possible. It's a digital ledger that records every transaction seamlessly.

Yes, blockchain can be theoretically hacked, but it is a complicated task to be achieved. A network of users constantly reviews it, which makes hacking the blockchain difficult.

Coinbase Global is currently the biggest blockchain company in the world. The company runs a commendable infrastructure, services, and technology for the digital currency economy.

Blockchain is a decentralized technology. It’s a chain of distributed ledgers connected with nodes. Each node can be any electronic device. Thus, one owns blockhain.

Bitcoin is a cryptocurrency, which is powered by Blockchain technology while Blockchain is a distributed ledger of cryptocurrency

Generally a database is a collection of data which can be stored and organized using a database management system. The people who have access to the database can view or edit the information stored there. The client-server network architecture is used to implement databases. whereas a blockchain is a growing list of records, called blocks, stored in a distributed system. Each block contains a cryptographic hash of the previous block, timestamp and transaction information. Modification of data is not allowed due to the design of the blockchain. The technology allows decentralized control and eliminates risks of data modification by other parties.

Blockchain has a wide spectrum of applications and, over the next 5-10 years, we will likely see it being integrated into all sorts of industries. From finance to healthcare, blockchain could revolutionize the way we store and share data. Although there is some hesitation to adopt blockchain systems right now, that won't be the case in 2022-2023 (and even less so in 2026). Once people become more comfortable with the technology and understand how it can work for them, owners, CEOs and entrepreneurs alike will be quick to leverage blockchain technology for their own gain. #9702. Artifact Immutability as a Release Primitive: Content Addressing, Digest Pinning, and the Substitution Attack Surface

Posted on Nov 12 • Originally published at neerajsinghi.com

Most teams treat image tags as release identifiers. They are not. A tag is a mutable pointer sitting on top of a content-addressed blob store. The digest—sha256:<64-hex>—is the identifier. Conflating the two produces a class of failure that looks like a deployment problem but is actually an artifact provenance problem: the rollback you thought was safe pulled a different image than the one you certified, the canary that passed load testing ran a different binary than production, or an attacker overwrote a tag between your CI scan and your Kubernetes pull.

This article examines what artifact immutability actually means in mechanical terms, where the guarantees break down, and how to enforce them across the CI/CD boundary without slowing rollouts.

An OCI image digest is the SHA-256 hash of the image manifest—not the layers, not the config blob, the manifest. The manifest references layers by their own digests. So the digest transitively covers the entire content graph, which means:

What the digest does not guarantee: it says nothing about what the image contains beyond content identity. A digest-pinned image can still carry a known CVE, a misconfigured binary, or a supply-chain-compromised base layer. Digest pinning is not a security policy; it is a consistency and reproducibility primitive on top of which you build policy.

Also worth stating plainly: client-side digest verification only works if the client checks. docker pull nginx:1.27 does not verify anything. docker pull nginx@sha256:abc123... instructs the registry to return a specific manifest, but the client must rehash the received manifest and compare. Container runtimes such as containerd do this by default for digest-referenced pulls; they do not do it for tag-referenced pulls where the registry resolves the tag server-side.

The scan and the deploy reference the same string, but if any of the following occur between push and deploy, the deployed image differs from the scanned one:

Scenario three is particularly subtle on Kubernetes. When a node's image is evicted and a pod reschedules to a new node, imagePullPolicy: IfNotPresent causes the new node to pull the tag fresh. If the tag has moved since original deployment, the new node runs a different image than the original nodes—silently.

The fix is mechanical: record the digest at push time and use only digests downstream.

The returned PushedArtifact.Digest becomes the canonical release identifier. Every downstream system—Helm values, Kubernetes manifests, rollback scripts—receives the digest, not the tag.

Recording digests in CI is necessary but insufficient if the deployment process can still reference tags. An admission webhook enforces the invariant at the cluster boundary.

The webhook inspects every Pod creation or update. If any container's image field resolves to a tag reference rather than a digest reference, the webhook rejects the pod.

This single check eliminates the entire class of tag-drift failures at admission time, before the kubelet ever contacts the registry. The tradeoff: your CD system must be capable of injecting digest references before submitting manifests. Kustomize image transformers and Helm post-render hooks both support this. If they do not fit, a mutating webhook that resolves tags to digests at admission is the fallback—but mutation is harder to audit than rejection.

Digest pinning proves content identity. It does not prove provenance—that the image was built by your CI system, with your Dockerfile, from your source commit. For that you need a signature.

Cosign's keyless signing mode, backed by Sigstore's Rekor transparency log and OIDC identity, attaches a signature to the image manifest without a separate key management burden. The signature is itself stored as an OCI artifact in the same registry, referenced by the image digest.

The verification gate belongs in two places: the CD pipeline before manifest generation, and the admission webhook before pod scheduling.

The latency cost of a Rekor lookup at admission time is real—typically 150–400 ms depending on the transparency log endpoint and your network topology. Options to manage it: cache verification results keyed by digest (digests are immutable, so a verified digest stays verified), use an in-cluster Rekor mirror, or move signature verification entirely to CD and make the webhook trust a verified-digest allowlist updated by CD. The allowlist approach introduces a synchronization hazard: if the allowlist update fails, no pods can schedule. Make the webhook fail-open for allowlist fetch errors with a compensating audit log, or accept fail-closed for high-security workloads.

Production registries are typically separate from CI build registries for security isolation. Artifact promotion—moving an image from a build registry to a staging registry to a production registry—must preserve digest identity, which requires content-addressed copying rather than re-pushing through a tag.

Tools like crane copy and skopeo copy copy by digest and preserve the manifest without rebuild. The digest of the artifact in the destination registry must be verified to match the source digest after copy. If it does not, the copy operation encountered a mid-flight corruption or the destination registry modified the manifest (some registries rewrite media types on ingest—this is a known incompatibility vector with older ECR behavior).

This verification step is frequently omitted and represents a silent integrity gap in most promotion pipelines.

Software Bill of Materials (SBOM) documents attached as OCI referrers are growing in regulatory relevance. The mechanical problem: an SBOM attached to an image digest is itself an OCI artifact, and its attachment is recorded in the referrers API response for that digest. If your promotion pipeline copies the image without copying its referrers, the SBOM does not follow the artifact into production.

crane copy --all and Oras copy with referrers support handle this, but not all registry implementations expose the referrers API consistently. Verify that your production registry supports the referrers API (GET /v2//referrers/) before depending on it in policy enforcement.

Apply these checks when designing your artifact delivery system:

1. Tag vs. digest in manifests. If any Kubernetes manifest in your production path references an image by tag, you have a reproducibility and drift risk. Enforce digest-only at admission or in the CD manifest generation step.

2. Post-push digest resolution. CI must resolve and record the digest immediately after push, before any downstream step runs. Treat the digest as the artifact ID for the rest of the pipeline.

3. Promotion integrity check. After every cross-registry copy, verify the destination digest matches the source. Fail the pipeline on mismatch.

4. Signature verification placement. Verify signatures in CD before manifest generation if latency at admission is unacceptable. Verify at admission if you want an enforcement point that CD bypasses cannot circumvent. Both when the threat model demands it.

5. Referrer completeness. If SBOMs or attestations are part of your compliance posture, confirm your registry supports the referrers API and that your promotion tooling copies referrers. Otherwise, attestations exist only in the build registry and are invisible in production.

6. Webhook failure policy. Fail-closed admission webhooks block all pod creation when the webhook is unavailable. Scope webhook coverage to namespaces that require it, keep the webhook stateless and fast, and define a runbook for webhook outage that does not involve disabling it silently.

Digest pinning is not a hardening step you add after the delivery system is built. It is the foundation on which reproducible, auditable, and safe artifact delivery is constructed. Every other control—signature verification, SBOM policy, rollback safety—depends on the artifact identifier being stable. Get that primitive right first.

Two hints for a better result: Mix the filling a day in advance to give the spices a chance to bloom, and be sure to remove the pie from the oven while the center is still wobbly, as overcooking it will cause the filling to crack.

Want even more spice in your pumpkin pie? This spice-forward recipe is for you. Using powerful Vietnamese cinnamon — with its more robust flavor profile — gives the pie an even spicier kick. Meanwhile, the filling is super silky-smooth thanks to a few tablespoons of corn syrup mixed in.

This beloved pie is made much like pumpkin pie, but with mashed sweet potatoes for nuanced flavor and heavy cream for an especially rich custard. This recipe takes classic pecan pie a step further by adding chocolate chips to the filling. The chocolate beautifully complements the pecans' nuttiness; if you choose bittersweet chocolate, it cuts the pie's overall sweetness, allowing all of the flavors to shine more brightly.

#9699. Offline-first Sync on Mobile: A Safe Migration Path

Posted on Nov 12 • Originally published at amitchakraborty.dev

Say you are a mobile app developer tasked with migrating your app's data synchronization mechanism from a traditional online-first approach to an offline-first approach. Your app relies heavily on syncing data between the client and server, and any downtime or data loss during the migration process could result in significant financial losses and damage to your user base. You've been trying to implement the new approach, but the complexity of the migration process and the risk of introducing bugs or data inconsistencies have been holding you back.

The traditional online-first approach to data synchronization assumes that the user always has a stable internet connection. However, in reality, mobile users often experience intermittent or slow connections, leading to data loss or inconsistencies. An offline-first approach, on the other hand, prioritizes the local data storage and synchronization, ensuring that the app remains functional even without a connection. However, migrating to this approach requires significant changes to the app's architecture, data models, and synchronization mechanisms.

To migrate to an offline-first approach without a freeze window, follow these steps:

The cost of migrating to an offline-first approach includes the time and resources required to redesign the data models, implement a local data store, and develop a synchronization mechanism. Additionally, the app may require significant testing and validation to ensure that the new approach works correctly. However, the benefits of an offline-first approach, including improved user experience, reduced data loss, and increased app reliability, often outweigh the costs.

When not to migrate to an offline-first approach:

When asked about migrating to an offline-first approach, a weak answer might focus on the technical details of the implementation without considering the trade-offs and potential issues. A strong answer, on the other hand, would discuss the benefits and costs of the migration, the potential risks and challenges, and the strategies for mitigating them.

Example question: "How would you migrate our app to an offline-first approach without disrupting the user base?" A weak answer: "I would use a library like React Query to handle data synchronization and caching." A strong answer: "I would first assess our current data model and identify the entities that need to be synchronized. Then, I would implement a local data store and develop a synchronization mechanism that can handle both online and offline modes. I would also consider the potential risks of data inconsistencies and conflicts, and develop strategies to mitigate them. Finally, I would test and validate the new approach to ensure that it works correctly and meets the user's expectations."

Follow-up question: "How would you handle conflicts between the local data store and the server?" A strong answer would discuss the strategies for resolving conflicts, such as last-writer-wins, multi-version concurrency control, or custom conflict resolution mechanisms, and explain the trade-offs between them.

Amit Chakraborty is a founding engineer and senior architect — React Native, AI/RAG systems and production architecture. Portfolio: www.amitchakraborty.dev · LinkedIn · GitHub. Open to senior and founding engineering roles, remote worldwide.

#9697. Most Frequently Asked Questions About Affiliate Marketing

Affiliate marketing is a way to make money by promoting the products and services of other people and companies. You don't need to create your product or service, just promote existing ones. That's why it's so easy to get started with affiliate marketing. You can even get started with no budget at all!

An affiliate program is a package of information you create for your product, which is then made available to potential publishers. The program will typically include details about the product and its retail value, commission levels, and promotional materials. Many affiliate programs are managed via an affiliate network like ShareASale, which acts as a platform to connect publishers and advertisers, but it is also possible to offer your program directly.

Affiliate networks connect publishers to advertisers.  Affiliate networks make money by charging fees to the merchants who advertise with them; these merchants are known as advertisers. The percentage of each sale that the advertiser pays is negotiated between the merchant and the affiliate network.

Dropshipping is a method of selling that allows you to run an online store without having to stock products. Commission rates are typically based on a percentage of the total sale and in some cases can also be a flat fee for each transaction. The rates are set by the merchant.
