#9696. How I Fold Thirty Reports of the Same Event Into One Story

Independent developer in Punjab, India. Building Hushread (hushread.com), an RSS and news reader with no algorithm.

Independent developer in Punjab, India. Building Hushread (hushread.com), an RSS and news reader with no algorithm.

Independent developer in Punjab, India. Building Hushread (hushread.com), an RSS and news reader with no algorithm.

When a ferry sinks or a central bank moves rates, thirty outlets publish within the hour. A normal RSS reader shows you thirty cards. I build Hushread, an RSS and news reader with no algorithm, and it shows that event once: one story, with a timeline of who reported what and when. This is how that grouping works, and where it went wrong on the way. Every number below is from the code as of October 2026.

Feeds wait in one queue ordered by when they were last pulled, so the feed that has waited longest goes next and a few busy sources can't hog the loop. Feeds people follow are pulled every 15 minutes. A source can be an RSS or Atom feed, a site without a feed, a subreddit, a YouTube channel or a public Facebook page; they all land in the same queue.

Each article is opened and cleaned to reader view (Mozilla Readability for the body, Defuddle for metadata and as the fallback) and dated from the feed or the page. If neither has a date, the date stays blank. Stamping "now" on an undated article makes old news look new, and grouping by time would then join things that never happened together.

Once a minute, new articles are embedded in one batched call. Each article then links to at most one earlier article from the previous 12 hours, when the two are close enough (cosine similarity 0.92 by default). That gives chains: article 12 points to 10, 10 points to 7. A chain is an event.

Chains beat re-clustering for one reason: they are cheap to keep correct while articles keep arriving. Each new article makes exactly one decision, and nothing already linked has to move.

The bug that taught me this: in October 2026 one article, "Netanyahu invites the pilot", sat close to two stories at once. It pulled a 90-article story about a Netanyahu visit to the UAE into a hijacking story. The two stories' centres were only 0.66 alike, while real fragments of the hijacking story sat at 0.73 to 0.86.

The fix was a rule, not a bigger model. One article may merge two stories only when the smaller one is still a fragment (8 articles or fewer, such as early or other-language copies) or when the two stories' centres agree (0.72 or more). Otherwise the article joins one story and leaves the other alone.

"Thirty articles" can be one outlet syndicated thirty times. A publisher is a normalised outlet name plus its domain, and a story's weight is the number of distinct publishers in it. Trending ranks stories by that count, never by clicks, and a story only trends once 5 or more different publishers cover it.

A written Story appears only when an event clears one of two bars:

Stories are written by an AI model from those outlets' reporting alone, and the page says so. Claims are attributed to the outlets that made them, every timeline entry links to the original report, and the byline is "Hushread Stories" with the number of outlets the piece was written from, because no person wrote it. While coverage continues, a Story takes a dated update when at least 2 new articles have arrived, at most every 6 hours.

A story closes after 48 quiet hours or at 7 days old. A closed story is linked to the one it follows when their centres are 0.78 alike or more and it still resembles the thread's first story (0.70). So "the next round of sanctions" joins the sanctions thread, while one football match doesn't swallow the next. Article, story, thread: the event, then the saga. Long stories show up as chapters, each with its own summary.

Independent developer in Punjab, India. Building Hushread (hushread.com), an RSS and news reader with no algorithm.

#9695. Lettering machine-translated manga: fitting text back into speech bubbles

When people think about translating manga automatically, they think about the translation model. In practice the translation is the easy part. The hard part is everything around it: finding the text, getting it off the page cleanly, and putting the translation back so the page still reads like a comic.

This post walks through the image side of an automatic manga translator I work on, and what we learned by comparing our pages with official English and Korean editions.

Translation sits between steps 3 and 5 and sees the whole page at once, so names and tone stay consistent from bubble to bubble.

The textbook answer is "mask the text and let an inpainting model fill the hole". On a plain white balloon that often leaves faint gray smudges where the letters used to be, and on screentone or detailed art it can invent texture that wasn't there.

What worked better for us was treating different backgrounds differently: plain paper, text with a white outline drawn over artwork, and text sitting on gradients or art each get their own handling. We also make sure that nothing outside the text area changes, so the art around a balloon stays exactly as the artist drew it.

Making text fit a box is easy. Making it look lettered is not. A few principles mattered most:

Most of the problems only show up at scale. A demo page looks fine; page 40 of a chapter is where a stray gray smudge, a hyphen in the wrong place or a bubble that's slightly too full gives it away. Comparing against official editions, page by page, taught us more than any metric did.

If you want to see the result on your own pages, Manga Translator is the web app built on this pipeline: upload a manga, manhwa or webtoon page in the browser and download it lettered in English or 50 other languages. I'd like to hear where the lettering still looks off.

#9690. TOP 11 AI MARKETING TOOLS YOU SHOULD USE (Updated 2022)

If you’re late to the AI party, don’t worry. It’s easier than you think to start leveraging artificial intelligence tools in your marketing strategy. Here are 11 AI marketing tools every marketer should start using today.

Personalize is an AI-powered technology that helps you identify and produce highly targeted sales and marketing campaigns by tracking the products and services your contacts are most interested in at any given time. The platform uses an algorithm to identify each contact’s top three interests, which are updated in real-time based on recent site activity.

Seventh Sense provides behavioral analytics that helps you win attention in your customers’ overcrowded email inboxes. Choosing the best day and time to send an email is always a gamble. And while some days of the week generally get higher open rates than others, you’ll never be able to nail down a time that’s best for every customer. Seventh Sense eases your stress of having to figure out the perfect send-time and day for your email campaigns. The AI-based platform figures out the best timing and email frequency for each contact based on when they’re opening emails. The tool is primarily geared toward HubSpot and Marketo customers

Phrasee uses artificial intelligence to help you write more effective subject lines. With its AI-based Natural Language Generation system, Phrasee uses data-driven insights to generate millions of natural-sounding copy variants that match your brand voice. The model is end-to-end, meaning when you feed the results back to Phrasee, the prediction model rebuilds so it can continuously learn from your audience.

HubSpot Search Engine Optimization (SEO) is an integral tool for the Human Content team. It uses machine learning to determine how search engines understand and categorize your content. HubSpot SEO helps you improve your search engine rankings and outrank your competitors. Search engines reward websites that organize their content around core subjects, or topic clusters. HubSpot SEO helps you discover and rank for the topics that matter to your business and customers.

When you’re limited to testing two variables against each other at a time, it can take months to get the results you’re looking for. Evolv AI lets you test all your ideas at once. It uses advanced algorithms to identify the top-performing concepts, combine them with each other, and repeat the process to achieve the best site experience.

Acrolinx is a content alignment platform that helps brands scale and improves the quality of their content. It’s geared toward enterprises – its major customers include big brands like Google, Adobe, and Amazon - to help them scale their writing efforts. Instead of spending time chasing down and fixing typos in multiple places throughout an article or blog post, you can use Acrolinx to do it all right there in one place. You start by setting your preferences for style, grammar, tone of voice, and company-specific word usage. Then, Acrolinx checks and scores your existing content to find what’s working and suggest areas for improvement. The platform provides real-time guidance and suggestions to make writing better and strengthen weak pages.

MarketMuse uses an algorithm to help marketers build content strategies. The tool shows you where to target keywords to rank in specific topic categories, and recommends keywords you should go after if you want to own particular topics. It also identifies gaps and opportunities for new content and prioritizes them by their probable impact on your rankings. The algorithm compares your content with thousands of articles related to the same topic to uncover what’s missing from your site.

Copilot is a suite of tools that help eCommerce businesses maintain real-time communication with customers around the clock at every stage of the funnel. Promote products, recover shopping carts and send updates or reminders directly through Messenger.

Yotpo’s deep learning technology evaluates your customers’ product reviews to help you make better business decisions. It identifies key topics that customers mention related to your products—and their feelings toward them. The AI engine extracts relevant reviews from past buyers and presents them in smart displays to convert new shoppers. Yotpo also saves you time moderating reviews. The AI-powered moderation tool automatically assigns a score to each review and flags reviews with negative sentiment so you can focus on quality control instead of manually reviewing every post.

Albert is a self-learning software that automates the creation of marketing campaigns for your brand. It analyzes vast amounts of data to run optimized campaigns autonomously, allowing you to feed in your own creative content and target markets, and then use data from its database to determine key characteristics of a serious buyer. Albert identifies potential customers that match those traits, and runs trial campaigns on a small group of customers—with results refined by Albert himself—before launching it on a larger scale.

Albert plugs into your existing marketing technology stack, so you still have access to your accounts, ads, search, social media, and more. Albert maps tracking and attribution to your source of truth so you can determine which channels are driving your business.

There are many tools and companies out there that offer AI tools, but this is a small list of resources that we have found to be helpful. If you have any other suggestions, feel free to share them in the comments below this article. As marketing evolves at such a rapid pace, new marketing strategies will be invented that we haven't even dreamed of yet. But for now, this list should give you a good starting point on your way to implementing AI into your marketing mix.

#9688. Is a gas oven bad for bread?: Why a gas oven may be interfering with your go-to steaming method.

Adapted from King Arthur Baking Company’s Big Book of Bread

One of the most crucial steps for making crusty artisan-style bread comes at the very end: steaming.

Baking bread with steam is critical for achieving expansive, open-crumbed loaves with a golden, crisp crust. If you bake bread in a dry oven, the crust quickly sets, which prevents the dough from expanding to its full potential; this, in turn, leads to loaves with a denser crumb. If you introduce steam at the start of the bake, the crust remains moist and pliable and the loaf can stretch and expand before the crust sets, resulting in a lighter, more open crumb.

What’s more, steam also helps gelatinize starches on the loaf’s exterior, which helps it brown and creates an especially crispy, flavorful, and shiny loaf. (Learn more: A guide to baking bread with steam at home.)

There are many different ways to steam your bread, all of which are designed to introduce moisture to the oven during the first part of baking. The most common method involves setting a large cast-iron skillet below your baking stone or steel when you preheat the oven. After you load your bread into the oven, you immediately pour a cup or so of warm water into the preheated cast-iron skillet and quickly close the door so the steam doesn’t escape.

This method works great, with one exception: It’s not effective in a gas oven.

If you have a gas oven, it’s very hard to add sufficient steam. By design, gas ovens vent out effluence, meaning whatever steam you add is very quickly vented out of the oven chamber. This is particularly true if you steam your bread by pouring hot water into a cast-iron skillet, as outlined above. All the water quickly dissipates, and there’s not enough moisture left to enhance the crust.

But all is not lost. There is a workaround.

If you’re steaming bread in a gas oven, you need to use a preheated covered baker, such as a Dutch oven. Instead of adding an additional water source, the lidded vessel traps the steam that escapes from the loaf as it bakes, becoming a kind of self-steaming oven. Because the steam is sealed in, the gas oven won’t vent it out.

You can use a Dutch oven for a round, boule-shaped loaf, or any other form of covered baker, like the Brod & Taylor Bread Steel for elongated, bâtard-shaped loaves. (There’s also a round version of the Bread Steel available.)

For more guidance on this method, see our previous blogs, Bread baking in a Dutch oven and For crispy, crackle crusts, put a lid on it.

When you load your dough into the oven, slip a few ice cubes between the parchment beneath your loaf and the pan to give the loaf an extra initial burst of steam. Just don’t skip the parchment beneath the dough. Otherwise, the extra water from the melting ice may cause your bread to stick to the pot.

#9686. I Turned U.S. Bitcoin Rules Into a One-Tap Game. Here’s What a Month of Building Taught Me

Disclosure: I built the game and write the newsletter mentioned in this story. Both are free. Nothing here is legal or tax advice.

This month I shipped a free browser game where every obstacle is a real U.S. Bitcoin rule. A set of free Bitcoin GIFs I publish passed 4.3 million views. And my plain legal explainers reached the top 2 of HackerNoon’s Web3 writer ranking.

Three very different formats. One lesson: information about the law spreads when it fits inside something people already do.

Here is what I built, how I built it, and what I learned.

For months I’ve been writing informative articles about Bitcoin law here on HackerNoon. No price talk, no predictions. Just how a specific rule works and who it affects.

This month, those articles put me in the top 2 of HackerNoon’s Web3 writers.

A small confession about that label. I’m a Bitcoin maxi, and “Web3” is not a word I would ever pick for myself. But it’s the category HackerNoon uses, and Bitcoin writers and Bitcoin stories are ranked inside it. So I’ll take the ranking and leave the label.

What I noticed is that the articles that travel are never the opinion pieces. They’re the precise ones. A form number, what it reports, who has to file it.

Articles have one limit. They only reach people who already want to read about regulation. Most Bitcoin holders don’t.

They will, however, play something for two minutes.

You’re an orange Bitcoin coin trying to reach cold storage. Tap to fly. Walls slide toward you, and every wall is labeled with a real U.S. rule or enforcement tool.

The others are Form 8300, the coffee tax, the 1040 question and an IRS letter.

Each gap you clear counts as one block. Every 21 blocks there’s a “halving” and the game speeds up.

Hit a wall and the run ends. The screen shows the rule that stopped you, one fact about it, and a link to the source. Ranks go from Paper Hands to Satoshi Tier.

There’s one power-up: a stamp marked WITHDRAWN that lets you pass through a single wall. It’s based on a real event. On October 5, FinCEN withdrew its 2020 proposal to require reports on transfers to self-hosted wallets.

Below the game, every wall is explained in plain English, with its source.

It had to be a real game. An earlier idea was closer to a quiz. I dropped it. Quizzes feel like homework, and nobody shares homework. Poor design is the usual reason gamified products fail, a point this gamification playbook makes well.

Every wall had to be real. Each one is a rule or event that exists, with a source you can check.

The game is a single static page. HTML canvas for the rendering, plain JavaScript, no framework, no backend. It sits on a static host under a subdomain. No server means nothing to maintain and nothing that logs visitors.

Gap positions are randomized and the order of the rules is shuffled on every run, so you can’t memorize a path. A player on X asked for a fixed practice mode so learning the rules feels less frantic. Fair point. It’s on the list.

The share flow taught me something about platforms. When a run ends, the game draws a square result card as a PNG, right in the browser. I wanted the “Share on X” button to attach that image automatically. It can’t. A website can prefill the text of a post, but not attach an image to it.

So the flow became: save the card, open the prefilled post, attach the image yourself. On phones, the button opens the system share sheet, which makes it almost seamless.

The third thing was never planned as a product.

I publish free Bitcoin GIFs on GIPHY. This month they passed 4.3 million views.

What I like most is where they end up. On X, bitcoiners use them in replies to explain an idea or make a point. Nobody visits a website to see them. They simply show up inside conversations that were already happening.

The articles, the game and the GIFs look unrelated. One is long-form text. One is a coin dodging tax forms. One is a few seconds of animation in a reply.

But they do the same job. Each one meets people where they already are, in an article feed, on a phone screen or in a thread on X, and hands them one accurate piece of information without asking for anything back.

If you write explainers of any kind, legal or technical, that’s the takeaway I’d offer. Stop waiting for people to come to the information. Put it inside the formats they already use.

And if you try the game, tell me in the comments which wall stopped you.

Disclosure: I built Cold Storage Run and write The Bitcoin Act, a free newsletter on Bitcoin law. Nothing in this story is legal or tax advice.

#9685. 116,000 Stars vs. One Binary: claude-mem and palace-rs, Fact by Fact

claude-mem is the most popular memory plugin for AI coding agents. At the time of writing it has 116,434 GitHub stars.

Stars tell you what people clicked. They don't tell you what you have to install, what runs in the background, who writes your memories, or whether anyone measured if the thing finds the right memory. So I went through both projects' own READMEs, docs and source and wrote down what each one actually does.

Every claim below links back to something you can open. No guesses.

claude-mem (from its README and package.json, v15.18.1):

That's a JavaScript runtime, a second JavaScript runtime, a Python toolchain, a vector database and a long-running HTTP service.

One binary, one SQLite file, no API keys, no cloud.

No Python, no vector database, no Docker. One palace executable and one palace.db file.

Embeddings run on your CPU through ONNX Runtime. There's no server process to keep alive. The install script downloads the release binary, verifies its SHA-256 checksum, and you run palace install to wire up your agents.

This is the biggest difference, and it's a design choice, not a detail.

claude-mem uses an LLM to write your memory. In its own words:

Hooks in your agent hand each tool call (what it reads, edits and runs) to a small local worker. A second agent turns that activity into short observations, and writes a summary when the session ends.

The default settings in SettingsDefaultsManager.ts are CLAUDE_MEM_PROVIDER: 'claude' and CLAUDE_MEM_MODEL: 'haiku'. So what ends up in memory is a model's summary of what happened, not what happened.

That second agent also has to be paid for by someone. The README lists three options: the hosted "claude-mem observer" (a 30-day free trial that asks for a payment method), your own OpenRouter or Gemini key, or your Anthropic plan. It then says:

With the observer, memory runs off-plan, so you get up to 100% more usage from your plan.

palace-rs stores text verbatim and uses no LLM.

Code, notes, and conversations are stored as written, not as an LLM summary that loses detail.

No API key, no model calls, no second agent, no subscription. Recall is hybrid search (BM25 fused with cosine similarity over local embeddings) plus intent-aware ranking. A local cross-encoder reranker is optional. Nothing in the memory path costs tokens to create.

A memory tool has one job: when the agent needs something from last week, return it.

palace-rs publishes its numbers. On LongMemEval s_cleaned (470 evaluated questions, each over a haystack of about 50 sessions and 115k tokens), stored the way Palace actually stores conversations:

From the README's method notes: "No LLM at any stage, no GPU." The one ranking weight picked on LongMemEval data was chosen on a different split (m_cleaned) and frozen before the run. Per-question-type results are published too, including the weakest category.

It also ships a coding-agent eval (51 questions like "why did we choose bundled sqlite?") that runs with one command:

The README says plainly that this eval is partly tuned, and prints the untuned numbers next to the tuned ones.

claude-mem's README publishes no retrieval benchmark. There's no LongMemEval score, no recall@K, no eval command. The token figures it does give ("~50-100 tokens/result" for the index, "~500-1,000 tokens/result" for full details) come with its own disclaimer:

The ratio is not a measured recall or end-to-end saving.

So for the most-starred memory tool in this space, there's no published number for how often it returns the right memory. For the 10-star one, there is, with the command to reproduce it.

Both tools use hooks. palace-rs installs four:

All hooks fail open: if the palace is missing or empty, the agent works as normal. Every result carries its wing, room, source file, drawer id and score breakdown, so you can see where an answer came from.

palace-rs has a temporal knowledge graph: subject → predicate → object, with a valid-from date. When a fact changes, the agent invalidates the old one and adds the new one, so the timeline keeps both. palace_conflicts flags facts that look stale or contradictory.

No telemetry. palace gain statistics are written to your local database only.

The only network calls are the one-time model download from Hugging Face and, if you turn it on, your own Palace Server in remote mode.

No account, no sign-in, no analytics. Back up with palace export or by copying palace.db. Delete everything by removing ~/.palace.

claude-mem is popular, and it covers a lot of agents. But popularity isn't architecture, and it isn't a benchmark.

Don't trust the stars. Don't trust me either. Every quote above is from the projects' own pages. Open them and check.

#9682. FileNotFoundError: [Errno 2] No such file or directory (Fix)

Posted on Nov 12 • Originally published at blog.emreguzel.ca

You run your script. Python stops and prints this:

But the file is sitting right there in your folder. So what's going on? Below are the six causes behind this error in real programs. Each one has the exact message it gives and a fix. I ran every example on Python 3.11, 3.12 and 3.14 on Windows. All three print the same message.

Your code called open(), and the operating system said it has no file at that path. Look at the end of the message. It shows the path exactly as Python got it, and that's your best clue. Either the name is wrong, or Python is searching a different folder than you think. A path like data.txt with no folder in front is a relative path. Python starts from the current working directory, not from the folder where your script lives. That one detail causes most of these errors.

Put three lines right before the open() that fails. They show where Python is looking, the full path it built, and whether that path exists:

Is the printed folder not the one holding your file? That's cause 1. Is the folder right? Then compare the file name letter by letter with a listing of the folder. That points to causes 2 and 3.

Here data.txt is next to the script. But you started the script from the folder above, for example with python wrong-working-directory/bug.py. Some editors do the same when you click Run, because they use the project root. Python then looks in the wrong place. The fix is to build the path from the script's own location. That doesn't care where you run it from:

scores.txt and score.txt are two different files. One missing letter is enough. So is a capital letter in the wrong place (names are case sensitive on Linux and macOS), or a space where an underscore should be. Check that the path exists before you open it. If it doesn't, print what's in the folder so the mistake jumps out:

Windows hides the extension of known file types by default. Say you save a file as notes.txt in Notepad. The real name can end up as notes.txt.txt, while Explorer shows notes or notes.txt. You can switch on File name extensions in the Explorer View menu. Or you can list the folder from Python, like in the fix below:

People get caught by this one. You're creating the file, so it feels like nothing needs to exist yet. But mode "w" makes the file and never the folders above it. Make the folder first. exist_ok=True keeps it from failing when the folder is already there. parents=True creates several levels at once:

In a terminal, ~ means your home folder. That's the shell doing the work, not the terminal itself. Python doesn't do it. So open("~/notes.txt") hunts for a folder literally named ~ inside the current directory. Expand it yourself:

Mode "r" is the default, and it only reads. Say your program creates a log or save file on its first run. Then the very first read fails, because nothing exists yet. Create the file if it's missing. Or open it with "a" (append), which creates it when needed:

Backslashes in a normal string are escape characters, and that bites on Windows. The path "notes\new_todo.txt" holds a newline, not the letters \n. You won't get FileNotFoundError here. I tested it, and Windows answers OSError: [Errno 22] Invalid argument. The cure is similar to the rest. Use a raw string (r"C:\temp\test.txt"), use forward slashes, or build the path with Path.

Use pathlib. Path(__file__).parent / "data" / "input.csv" gives you the right path on every system. It doesn't depend on the working directory. Check before you open. Path.exists() and Path.is_file() let you print a clear message instead of a traceback. Catch the error where a missing file is normal, like a settings file on the first run. Handle only that case:

FileNotFoundError: [Errno 2] means the path Python built doesn't exist. So print the working directory and the resolved path. Compare them with where the file really is. Then stop relying on relative names, and build paths from the script's location with pathlib.

Want more Python errors with a clear cause? Try KeyError in Python, ValueError: invalid literal for int(), IndexError: List Index Out of Range and ModuleNotFoundError After pip install. New to Python? Start with Python for Beginners.

Download the code: the broken and fixed versions of all six causes are on GitHub in Python-projects/Troubleshooting/filenotfounderror. Run any file with python bug.py from inside its folder. The exception is wrong-working-directory, which you run from the folder above it.

#9678. AI Automation Safety: When to Keep a Human in the Loop

Founder of Amplence. I build custom AI agents and n8n automations for small and mid-size businesses, and write about keeping AI agents reliable and

Founder of Amplence. I build custom AI agents and n8n automations for small and mid-size businesses, and write about keeping AI agents reliable and

Founder of Amplence. I build custom AI agents and n8n automations for small and mid-size businesses, and write about keeping AI agents reliable and

My rule for every AI workflow we build: the AI never pays or deletes on its own, and it only sends what a person has already decided is safe to send. Routine, tested cases go out automatically. Anything involving money, a judgment call or a step you can't take back stops and waits for a person.

I run Amplence, a small AI automation agency, and I've been building software and automations for clients since 2018. Most of what we automate runs without anyone touching it. But I've learned that not everything that can be automated should be. The steps I'm most careful with are the ones you can't take back.

This post covers how we decide which steps get a human approval, two lessons from a live client system, an invoice-approval template I built, what we do when a model is retired, and how to build the approval step in Zapier with Human in the Loop.

A step gets an approval when a wrong run is expensive and can't be reversed. We ask three questions about every step that acts on the outside world:

If the answer to the first question is no, and either of the other two points to risk, a person approves it. In practice, that sorts most steps like this:

Tag an incoming email by language and topic

Remove records, cancel orders, archive accounts

The approval isn't a sign that the AI is bad. It's a sign that the action is permanent.

CollageDepot is a Shopify store whose customers write in Dutch, English, German and French. We spent two months building an AI email system that handles that inbox.

The workflow does the slow parts on its own. It reads each incoming email, detects the language, looks up the order in Shopify and drafts a reply in the customer's own language. It also applies the store's material-specific rules, so the answer about one product doesn't get copied onto another.

Not every email gets the same treatment. Routine questions that match the cases we tested are answered automatically, which covers about 65% of the 5,000-plus emails the store gets each month. The rest, including anything judgment-heavy, unclear or touching money like a refund or a return, goes to a person in a review dashboard in Airtable instead of getting a confident guess.

That split is what made the client comfortable going live. The AI handles the volume in four languages, and a person still decides every case where a wrong answer would cost money or trust. A person set the rules for what goes out automatically, and the AI doesn't get to widen them.

In September 2026, the CollageDepot workflow stopped reading email for part of a day while still showing as active. Nothing errored. The dashboard looked healthy. No new emails were being picked up.

The cause was the connection to the mailbox. The workflow listens to the inbox over IMAP, and it was set to force a reconnect. One of those reconnects failed silently. The workflow stayed switched on, but it was listening to a connection that no longer existed.

Floris, the client, spotted it in under a day. We had no alert for it. Because nothing was being processed at all, nothing wrong was sent to anyone, and the only damage was slower replies. We removed the faulty reconnect setting, and the listener has been stable since.

The lesson I took from it: "active" is not the same as "working." A status light tells you the workflow is switched on, not that it's doing anything. If a workflow normally handles something every hour, check for output, not status. A simple scheduled check that alerts you when nothing has come through in a few business hours catches this kind of silent failure long before a customer does.

This one isn't a client system. It's an invoice-approval template I built, and the rule at its center works in any tool: when an invoice arrives with bank details that don't match what's on file for that supplier, the workflow holds it. It doesn't pay, and it doesn't update the supplier's record. A person checks it first.

This is one of the most common ways businesses lose money to email fraud. Someone gets into a supplier's mailbox, or fakes one, and sends a normal-looking invoice with a new account number. An AI reading that invoice will extract the new details perfectly. It has no way to know they're wrong.

So the workflow does the reading and the comparison, and the person does the judgment:

The hold costs a day at most. Paying a fraudster costs the whole invoice, and that money rarely comes back.

AI providers retire models on their own schedule, and the workflow has to move to a newer one. We treat that switch as a new release, not a settings change, and re-testing a client build takes us roughly three weeks.

A newer model isn't simply a better version of the old one. It can phrase things differently, follow a rule a little more loosely, change the length or format of its output, or handle one language better and another worse. In a support workflow that answers in four languages, any of those can quietly change what customers read.

This is where the approval step earns its keep a second time. The hard cases already go to a person, and during the re-test the new model's output is reviewed before it's trusted to send anything on its own.

Zapier's Human in the Loop pauses a Zap until a person responds, then continues or stops based on their answer. Here's the invoice check from Case 3 as a Zap:

The settings matter more than the step itself. For anything that moves money, this is how we set the Request Approval action:

"Bank details changed for this supplier. Confirm by phone using the number on file before approving."

Puts the check in front of the reviewer every time

Supplier, amount, invoice number, old bank details, new bank details

The reviewer sees the change side by side

Bank details should come from the supplier, not be typed in by the reviewer

Never "Skip and continue" on a payment step: silence must not count as yes

After the reviewer responds, later steps can use the Decision field and any Reviewer Note. Every approval and decline is also logged in the Zap's change history, which gives you an audit trail of who approved what.

The same pattern works for the other cases. For a customer reply, use Request Approval with Let Reviewer edit content? set to Yes, so the reviewer can fix the draft before it sends. For a delete or cancel step, set the timeout to end the run, just like a payment.

Let the AI do the reading and drafting. Keep a person on the steps you can't take back. Before you switch a step to fully automatic, check:

The goal isn't to slow automation down. It's to make it safe enough that clients trust it with the rest of their work.

Founder of Amplence. I build custom AI agents and n8n automations for small and mid-size businesses, and write about keeping AI agents reliable and

#9676. ValueError: invalid literal for int() with base 10 (Fix)

Posted on Nov 12 • Edited on Nov 12 • Originally published at blog.emreguzel.ca

Your script runs, then Python stops with this:

You gave int() a string that doesn't look like a whole number. The end of the message shows the exact text Python choked on, in quotes. So the error already tells you what's wrong. Below are the six inputs that cause it most often, and how to fix each one. I ran every example on Python 3.11, 3.12 and 3.14. All three print the same message.

int(text) turns a string like "42" into the number 42. It takes an optional sign and digits. It also ignores spaces and a newline at either end, so int(" 42\n") works. Anything else breaks it: a decimal point, a comma, a letter, an empty string. Python raises a ValueError for those. Why not a TypeError? Because a string is the right type. This particular value just isn't usable.

The real cause is where the string came from. Text from input(), a file line, a CSV cell, a web form or an API is always text. And text can hold anything.

Look at the quoted text at the end of the message. That's the string that failed. If it might hide odd characters, print it with repr():

Then compare what you see with the six cases below.

The message ends in : '', with nothing between the quotes. You'll see it when someone hits Enter at an input() prompt. You'll also see it with an empty CSV cell, or when a split line leaves an empty piece. Catch the error, then decide what an empty value should mean:

Odd, but true: int() happily takes the float 3.5 and cuts it to 3. It refuses the string "3.50". So go through a float first. For money, use decimal and skip the rounding surprises:

Numbers pasted from a web page or spreadsheet often carry commas. Strip them before you convert. Does your data use a space or a dot instead? Remove that one:

Values like 72kg, $5 or 50% have characters that aren't digits. Pull the digits out with a regular expression. Or strip the symbol if you know exactly what it is. Check the regex actually found something, since re.search gives back None when it doesn't:

Unless you say otherwise, int() reads base 10. That's why the message says with base 10. Hex text like "ff" needs the base as a second argument. Use 16 for hex, 2 for binary and 8 for octal:

Reading a file line by line? The first line is often a title or header, not data. The message names the culprit, here 'id'. Skip that line. Or let the csv module deal with the header for you:

If a person typed the text, don't assume it's a number. Keep asking until it is:

Put only the conversion inside try. That way an unrelated bug won't get swallowed by the same except. And don't rely on text.isdigit() alone. It rejects negatives like "-5", and it says True for some characters that int() can't convert.

float() acts the same way, with a different message: ValueError: could not convert string to float: 'abc'. The causes match too. Think empty strings, a comma as the decimal mark ("3,5"), a unit or symbol, or a header. The fixes above work here as well.

A few string methods fix most messy input in one line. strip() trims spaces and newlines from both ends, though int() already ignores those. replace() removes separators. split() cuts a line into pieces, and you convert each piece on its own. A small helper keeps all the cleaning in one place:

Python also allows underscores inside a number, so int("1_000") is 1000. The language permits it. Still, a stray underscore in user input is more likely a typo, so the helper removes it. Returning a default instead of raising is a choice, too. Make it only where you know what a bad value should mean for your program.

ValueError: invalid literal for int() with base 10 means the string isn't a plain whole number. The message ends with that exact string, so read it first. Then clean it, convert it the right way, or validate before converting. And wrap only the conversion in try/except ValueError.

Other Python errors with a clear cause are IndexError: List Index Out of Range, TypeError: NoneType Is Not Subscriptable, IndentationError and UnboundLocalError. New to Python? Start with Python for Beginners.

Download the code: the broken and fixed versions of all six causes are on GitHub in Python-projects/Troubleshooting/valueerror-invalid-literal-int. Run any file with python bug.py from inside its folder.

#9674. ZIG Finance Opens $100M Vault to Bring Saudi Arabia's SME Lending Boom Onchain

AI, Web3, Cybersecurity, Startup Funding & Enterprise SaaS. Top Journalist, Analyst & Thought Leadership Media Leader.

AI, Web3, Cybersecurity, Startup Funding & Enterprise SaaS. Top Journalist, Analyst & Thought Leadership Media Leader.

AI, Web3, Cybersecurity, Startup Funding & Enterprise SaaS. Top Journalist, Analyst & Thought Leadership Media Leader.

Private credit, the business of lending to companies outside the public bond market and the banking system, has grown into a market of more than $2 trillion that Moody's expects to approach $4 trillion by 2030. A growing slice of it now lives onchain. Private credit makes up about 44% of the $51 billion market for tokenized real-world assets, which puts roughly $22 billion of loans on public blockchains, while onchain private credit grew about 180% in a year to early 2026.

Saudi Arabia is one of the fastest-growing credit markets feeding that demand. Lending to Saudi small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) reached SR468 billion, or about $124.6 billion, at the end of 2025, up 33% in a year, while Vision 2030 aims to lift SMEs' share of total credit from 11.5% to 20%. Global institutions have had few direct routes into those loans, since most are made by local banks and lending platforms.

ZIG Finance launched the zEMS Vault on 11 November 2026 to open that route. The vault gives eligible institutional investors exposure to a diversified pool of Saudi SME private credit on BNB Chain, with subscriptions and redemptions in stablecoins. It is the first product from ZIG Finance's strategic partnership with Laser Digital, the digital assets subsidiary of Japanese bank Nomura, which acts as risk framework advisor, while the zEMS onchain strategy targets a raise of $100 million.

Private credit has been one of the fastest-growing asset classes since the 2008 financial crisis, as banks pulled back from riskier lending and specialist funds stepped in. Moody's puts global assets under management at more than $2 trillion, with a forecast of close to $4 trillion by 2030, as insurers, pension funds and wealthy investors look for income above public bond yields.

Tokenization, the process of recording ownership of an asset as a digital token on a blockchain, is bringing that market to new investors. Private credit overtook US Treasury products in 2026 to become the largest category of tokenized real-world assets, at about 44% of the market against 30% for Treasuries, with the total market up 42% so far in 2026. Onchain private credit products have typically offered yields of about 8% to 12%, compared with 4% to 5% for tokenized Treasuries, which explains the appetite.

Saudi lending to SMEs has grown at one of the fastest rates of any major credit market. Credit to micro, small and medium enterprises rose from SR307.4 billion in the second quarter of 2024 to SR351.7 billion by the end of that year, then to SR420.7 billion by mid-2025 and SR468 billion by the end of 2025. That is a 52% rise in 18 months (our arithmetic), while SMEs' share of total credit climbed from about 9.6% to 11.5%.

The growth is driven by Vision 2030, Saudi Arabia's economic plan, which aims to lift the SME share of credit to 20% and SMEs' contribution to GDP to 35%. Banks provide about 95% of SME credit today, with financing companies providing the rest, which leaves wide room for non-bank lenders and outside investors as the target approaches. Reaching 20% from 11.5% means SME credit has to keep growing faster than total lending for years.

Private credit is becoming a major source of growth capital across the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC), the six-country bloc that includes Saudi Arabia and the UAE. Private debt deployed in the region grew from about $0.5 billion in 2024 to $4.1 billion in 2025, overtaking venture capital at $3.3 billion, while Saudi Arabia accounted for about $3.9 billion of the total.

The demand is far larger than the supply. GCC SMEs face a credit gap of more than $250 billion, with SMEs receiving less than 10% of bank lending across the region, while global managers including King Street have announced plans to deploy billions in Saudi private credit. Industry estimates expect Gulf private credit to grow 15% to 30% a year over the next five years, as Fortune has noted in its coverage of the region.

The vault is issued by a segregated portfolio of ZM Structured Products SPC Limited, a company in the British Virgin Islands whose segregated portfolios keep each product's assets and liabilities separate. Merritt Administrators, which trades as ZIG Finance and is an authorized financial services provider regulated by South Africa's Financial Sector Conduct Authority, acts as curator. Investors hold vault tokens and do not own the underlying loans directly.

Each partner covers one part of the chain. Beehive originates the loans, Zamanat structures the product and provides Sharia advisory so it can meet Islamic finance principles, Laser Digital supports the design of the risk governance framework and gives tokenization advice, while ZIG Markets handles issuance, curation and distribution on BNB Chain. KAIO, the tokenization platform built by Laser Digital and WebN, runs tokenization, compliance and lifecycle management, including know-your-customer (KYC) checks at subscription and redemption.

The structure is also expected to include Khalij as the Sharia certification partner, with an independent calculation agent to be appointed separately. A Sharia-aligned structure opens the vault to investors who follow Islamic finance rules, a pool that the Islamic Financial Services Board puts at about $4.4 trillion of industry assets in 2025.

Beehive brings the lending base. Founded in Dubai in 2014, it was the first peer-to-peer lending platform in the Middle East and North Africa to be regulated by the Dubai Financial Services Authority. It has funded more than $1 billion for more than 2,100 SMEs across the UAE, Saudi Arabia and Oman. Its Saudi entity is subject to regulatory approval, while its UAE and Oman businesses are regulated by the DFSA and Oman's FSA.

KAIO brings the onchain rails. The platform has transacted more than $500 million in volume across more than 10 blockchains, with institutional funds from partners including BlackRock, Brevan Howard, Hamilton Lane, Laser Digital and Mubadala Capital live on it. Laser Digital, which Nomura set up to bridge traditional and crypto markets, is regulated by Dubai's VARA and ADGM's FSRA and registered with Japan's FSA.

ZIG Finance ties the pieces together. Its ecosystem includes ZIGChain, a layer 1 blockchain built for institutional finance, ZIG Markets as its distribution layer and the ZIG token. Laser Digital became a strategic investor and risk partner in ZIGChain in August 2026, with the two companies setting a target of at least $100 million in total value locked across several onchain credit products.

The vault launches on BNB Chain, one of the most active networks for tokenized assets. Real-world assets on the chain grew from about $3 billion in March 2026 to $5.2 billion in July, a 73% rise in four months (our arithmetic), making it the second-largest RWA network behind Ethereum with a 14.9% share.

The vault's design is about managing credit risk in the open. ZIG Finance's stated aim is to make the risk of lending to Saudi SMEs transparent and manageable, so institutional investors can get comfortable with an asset class they could not otherwise access at scale. Laser Digital's role is to help design ZIG Finance's own risk framework and the tokenization and issuance structure, with responsibility for credit selection and risk management resting with ZIG Finance and the originator.

The product carries the risks of any private credit investment. The vault does not guarantee returns, is not principal-protected and is not a deposit, while credit risk remains tied to the underlying SME borrowers. Laser Digital and Nomura do not guarantee, underwrite or rate the loans. The product is available only to eligible institutional investors in selected jurisdictions, excluding US persons and residents of Canada and Australia.

The zEMS Vault is the first product milestone in ZIG Finance's partnership with Laser Digital, which targets a minimum of $100 million in total value locked across multiple product rollouts. The companies describe the vault's architecture as a template that can be applied to other emerging markets and credit strategies, combining local origination with institutional risk governance, compliant tokenization and broader distribution.

Further opportunities across the region and other asset classes are already under consideration. A $100 million raise would equal about 10% of the more than $1 billion Beehive has funded since 2014 and about 0.08% of Saudi SME credit outstanding (our arithmetic), which shows how much room the model has to grow if it works.

Saudi SME credit is growing by tens of billions of riyals a year, Gulf private debt grew eightfold in 2025 and tokenized private credit has become the largest category of onchain real-world assets. The zEMS Vault sits where those three trends meet, giving global institutions a regulated, Sharia-aligned and stablecoin-settled route into a market that has mostly been funded by local banks.

The first test is the $100 million raise and how the loan pool performs through its first cycles. If the structure gains traction, ZIG Finance and Laser Digital plan to apply the same model to more GCC and emerging-market credit, turning a single vault into a pipeline that connects local lenders with global onchain capital.

This article is for information only and does not constitute investment advice or an offer of any product. The zEMS Vault is available only to eligible institutional investors in eligible jurisdictions, does not guarantee returns and carries the risk of loss of the entire investment.

#9673. This fall, reach for this unlikely apple ingredient : Apple cider vinegar is a baker’s secret weapon.

As fall baking season settles in, you're probably reaching for apples — and the many flavor-packed ingredients they produce. Applesauce cooks down into tangy apple butter to be cradled in a flaky galette, while a drop of boiled cider can deliver supercharged apple flavor to crumb cake. But the baking ingredient you may be overlooking may be something you associate more with salad dressings and wellness tonics: apple cider vinegar.

This tangy, apple-y vinegar is a secret ingredient in some of our favorite fall recipes, including cookbook author Claire Saffitz’s Cinnamon-and-Sugar Apple Pie. While lemon juice is the standard acid used in most fruit pie fillings, Claire opts for apple cider vinegar here to complement the filling’s flavors. “It helps as a flavor enhancer, and I also like that it’s apple cider in an apple pie. It’s a nice symmetry,” she mentions.

Similarly, apple cider vinegar is used in the cooking liquid alongside sugar and butter to caramelize apples in a Classic Apple Tarte Tatin. The benefit is twofold: Vinegar’s acidity helps cut the sweetness of the caramel, and it prevents the apples from getting too mushy, instead maintaining their fork-tender texture.

Pastry chef and cookbook author Natasha Pickowicz often leans into the jolt vinegar can add, including adding a few drops to her cake soaks for an additional layer of flavor. “Cake soaks should have a balance of tart, sweet, and savory notes — just like vinaigrette for your favorite salad,” she writes in her cookbook More Than Cake. It can add intrigue to layered cakes like this Golden Spice Cake or Pumpkin Layer Cake. In her cookbook, she also calls for a glaze spiked with apple cider vinegar to brush onto an apple tart after baking. It’s the finishing touch “to further emphasize the tart’s resolute apple-ness,” she writes.

Apple cider vinegar doesn’t need to be limited to only apple desserts, either. In our Old-Fashioned Pecan Pie, we call for apple cider vinegar as a foil to the brown sugar filling’s cloying sweetness. A spoonful of apple cider vinegar may not announce itself boldly, but it makes a small splash for brighter, more balanced bakes.

#9667. Scrambled Eggs Are 10x Creamier & Fluffier With One Boxed Ingredient

When you make scrambled eggs, heat, fat content, and your tools often require you to make them either fluffy or creamy, not both. However, powdered milk is an interesting ingredient that can help you bridge the divide, imparting richness and enabling volume, provided you use it correctly.

Powdered milk can be made from skim milk, whole milk, and buttermilk, but all are essentially just milk with the water taken out and converted into a soluble powder. When it comes to water versus milk in scrambled eggs, folks typically favor the latter because it gives a bit of extra richness and flavor. However, it can weigh them down, unlike water, which steams to fluff up the little curds into pillowy softness. While you can't just add water to powdered milk eggs because you'd just be using milk with extra steps, it does allow you to employ other tricks that increase the fluffiness, giving you the best of both worlds.

Powdered milk is also quite a bit more convenient since it's shelf-stable and dry. Not only does it last longer than regular milk, but you can also toast the powder to lend a nutty savoriness similar to browned butter. Roughly a tablespoon per three eggs is all you need to achieve serious flavor. Nonfat varieties typically last much longer than full-fat varieties, which tend to have a shorter shelf life. Freezing it can extend its shelf life even further, so it's an easy and cheap ingredient to keep on hand.

The biggest benefit of powdered versus liquid milk is that it adds milk solids without adding extra water. This helps you avoid making your scrambled eggs too watery and is why, while it may not make them fluffy on its own, it also won't inhibit other tricks. There's no shortage of expert tips for restaurant-quality eggs, but try focusing on ones that add a bit of extra air and/or cook them quickly for the best results.

You'll want to thoroughly incorporate your powdered milk, but luckily, a thorough whisking also helps introduce some air into the eggs. The goal is to make your mixture paler and more voluminous, looking as if you added extra liquid. The mason jar hack of shaking your eggs is not only easier than learning a fancy technique, but also helps ensure your powder is dispersed properly. If you're making a ton, you can even repurpose a protein shaker bottle and let that little metal whisk ball do the heavy lifting for you.

Slowly bringing your eggs to temperature is a French style that gives them a creamy, porridge-like consistency. However, this also slowly coagulates the proteins and prevents them from fluffing up properly. The key is to cook them fast enough that their natural moisture steams, but not so hot that they turn rubbery. Full-fat milk powder can help contribute to a tender texture and, when used in conjunction with moderate heat, help produce eggs that are moist but fluffy, creamy but firm.

#9666. Beyond Fiber Optics: The Hardware Reality of a Decentralized Internet

Tech enthusiast & writer exploring AI algorithms, quant models, and decentralized technology.

Tech enthusiast & writer exploring AI algorithms, quant models, and decentralized technology.

Tech enthusiast & writer exploring AI algorithms, quant models, and decentralized technology.

In its 2023 report, the digital rights group Access Now documented 283 internet shutdowns across 39 countries. While this figure includes targeted platform blocking rather than just total national blackouts, it highlights a stark reality: various state actors and conflicting parties hold the ultimate trump card. They can simply issue administrative orders to local telecom operators to restrict routing or suspend connectivity.

Web3 developers have spent years bulletproofing consensus mechanisms and peer-to-peer storage. Yet, if the physical fiber-optic cables belong to a state monopoly, software encryption cannot protect network availability. Furthermore, even when physical lines remain active, governments can compel ISPs to execute software-level blocks like SNI (Server Name Indication) filtering. Whether through severing physical connections or enforcing digital filters at the ISP level, access to even the most decentralized dApp becomes severely restricted for average users.

This physical bottleneck highlights the core motivation behind Decentralized Physical Infrastructure Networks (DePIN). Projects in the satellite space, including Spacecoin, are engineering architectures to decouple network access from terrestrial telecoms. However, bypassing legacy ISPs is not an absolute cure for censorship—it merely shifts the battleground from software firewalls to hardware logistics.

Many assume that orbital networks bypass terrestrial laws entirely, but Starlink’s recent legal battle in Brazil illustrates the limitations of centralized physical infrastructure.

After the Brazilian Supreme Court ordered X (formerly Twitter) blocked, Starlink initially refused to comply. After Justice Alexandre de Moraes froze Starlink's local accounts over potential liability for fines owed by X, Starlink notified the telecom regulator that it would comply with the court's blocking order. While Starlink publicly maintained that the asset freeze was illegal, this chronological sequence of events underscores how operating as a centralized corporate entity with a vulnerable financial footprint creates distinct compliance chokepoints.

Web3 infrastructure projects aim to solve this by separating the coordination protocol from physical data routing. However, it is crucial to distinguish between protocol decentralization and physical hardware ownership. According to deployment updates, Spacecoin's CTC-0 nanosatellite launched in December 2024, followed by three CTC-1 satellites in November 2025. These satellites are physically owned and operated by a traditional corporate entity (Space Telecommunications Inc.).

The Spacecoin protocol does not decentralize the physical satellite ownership. Instead, its technical roadmap outlines a separation of capabilities. According to Spacecoin's official updates, its protocol is designed to manage authorization, authentication, and accounting across the decentralized infrastructure, while smart contracts and crypto payments support bandwidth coordination. However, the extent to which these capabilities are operational in the deployed satellite network remains distinct from the protocol's stated design.

On October 1, 2025, Spacecoin claimed a successful demonstration using its CTC-0 satellite to transmit secured data over 7,000 kilometers between Chile and the Azores. While Spacecoin has since announced regional connectivity pilots and commercial partnerships in 2026, a globally resilient, independently accessible satellite internet service remains a different milestone from its initial proofs of concept.

Treating orbital networks as an instant bypass for censorship ignores how physical infrastructure is regulated. Moving the internet to an orbital mesh introduces distinct vectors for state control.

Space is borderless, but RF (Radio Frequency) spectrum is strictly policed. Transmitting high-speed data to orbit typically involves licensed spectrum, such as Ku, Ka, L, or S bands. Legally utilizing these frequencies requires two distinct regulatory processes: international coordination through the ITU for frequency assignments and orbital positions—including procedures intended to prevent harmful interference—and separate national authorizations granted by local communications regulators within their jurisdictions. If a decentralized project operates outside authorized spectrum allocations or exceeds the technical limits applicable to license-exempt ISM bands, state actors may treat the transmissions as unlawful. Governments do not necessarily need to attack the blockchain; they can confiscate unauthorized hardware or, in specific scenarios, attempt to deploy localized radio jamming equipment to disrupt targeted frequencies.

While downloading data via a passive receiver can sometimes go unnoticed, two-way satellite internet requires user terminals to transmit data back to orbit. These uplink transmissions emit RF signatures that, with specialized equipment, can potentially be detected and localized. Regimes can outlaw the import and possession of unauthorized satellite terminals. If customs agencies seize the hardware at the border, it can severely restrict network deployment before a single node comes online.

Launching nanosatellites and manufacturing custom RF receivers requires massive upfront capital. If a decentralized network relies on a small number of aerospace launch providers or hardware manufacturers to deploy its infrastructure, those companies become the new chokepoints. A state actor merely needs to apply regulatory pressure on the hardware manufacturers or impose import restrictions to cripple the network's expansion.

Decentralized physical infrastructure does not erase state control. Instead, it forces a shift in the logistics of executing it.

Today, restricting internet access is a relatively straightforward administrative task that relies on legal mandates enforced through local regulators, government agencies, and compliant telecom operators. Censoring a blockchain-coordinated satellite network, however, expands the required enforcement toolkit. It creates a scenario where a state might be forced to strictly police domestic hardware supply chains and import channels, actively track localized RF uplinks, or seize physical terminals.

A decentralized physical internet does not stop governments from using inexpensive software blocks; rather, it introduces a reality where regimes may have to supplement digital firewalls with highly visible, financially exhausting physical enforcement.

#9664. What is high-extraction flour, exactly?  : A baker’s guide to our new T85 Baker's Reserve Bread Flour.

High-extraction flour is a technical term that often prompts a lot of confusion from those unfamiliar with it. But with the debut of our new high-extraction flour, known as Baker’s Reserve Bread Flour, we’re breaking down just what it is and why it's a great choice for avid bread makers.

The extraction rate of a flour refers to how much of the original grain — the bran, germ, and endosperm — ends up in the final flour. A high-extraction flour typically has an extraction rate of about 80% to 90%, meaning some of the bran and germ have been sifted out, but it still retains much of the original grain. Our Baker’s Reserve Bread Flour is a T85 flour, meaning its extraction rate is 85%.

To put that in perspective, whole wheat flour has an extraction rate of 100%; it retains the entirety of the grain, including the bran, germ, and endosperm.

High-extraction flour falls between white and whole wheat flour. It’s lighter and less coarse than whole wheat flour because some of the bran has been sifted out, but it still retains more flavor, nutrients, and color than white flour, since it retains much of the original grain.

High-extraction flour is popular for artisan bread baking because it offers a balance of nutrition and good gluten development. It’s great for rustic loaves, baguettes, and pizza dough, and particularly well-suited for sourdough baking because it strikes a balance between flavor, nutrition, fermentation, and dough strength.

You can substitute our Baker’s Reserve Bread Flour 1:1 for bread flour (by weight or volume) in artisanal bread recipes; it can also be used 1:1 to replace the total flour in recipes that call for a combination of all-purpose and whole wheat flour. If you're subbing Baker’s Reserve Bread Flour for all-purpose flour in a bread recipe, you may find you need to add slightly more liquid to the recipe.

Bread bakers love high-extraction flour for artisan bread and sourdough because it offers the flavor and nutrition of whole grain flour; the stronger gluten development and more open crumb you get from white flour; and better fermentation from the minerals present in the bran and germ, which feed the wild yeast and lactic acid bacteria in sourdough starter, promoting more active fermentation.

If you want a loaf of bread that’s more flavorful and nutritious than bread made with exclusively white flour, but that still rises high and has an open crumb, high-extraction flour is a great choice.

Yes — in fact, it’s a great choice for feeding starter because of the sourdough-friendly minerals present in the flour, which boost activity in your starter.

Yes! T85 is a French specification that refers to the extraction rate (85%) of the flour. Our Baker’s Reserve Bread Flour is a T85 flour, meaning the extraction rate is 85%. If you have a recipe that calls for T85, this flour is the perfect choice.

Find our high-extraction Baker’s Reserve Bread Flour online.

#9662. Give Onion Rings A Protein Boost With This Breakfast Side

Pairing your onion rings with a meaty ingredient doesn't just infuse them with umami, but can also make them a meal in their own right. Bacon-wrapped onion rings, in particular, are relatively straightforward to put together and have roughly 3 to 4 grams of protein per piece (depending on how much bacon each ring uses).

Onions already have a dose of fiber, potassium, and vitamins C and B6, so adding some extra protein can give you something with a more comprehensive nutritional profile. While exact quantities vary based on the type, cut, and marbling of the bacon you use, meat is a "complete protein," meaning it contains all nine essential amino acids necessary for good health. Since this recipe doesn't call for deep-frying, it's not only easier, but also a good alternative for those attempting to reduce their consumption of vegetable-based oils. You won't even have to make sure any breading sticks, so it's a protein-laden option for those who want a bit of indulgence but steer clear of starches and grains.

The recommended minimum dietary allowance for protein is 0.36 grams per pound of body weight, so getting your necessary amount every day can be a challenge. Finding little ways to introduce more into your diet, especially complete proteins, is a solid way to achieve this. Since leftover bacon reheats quite well, it's easy to make a batch of these onion rings ahead of time and have little protein snacks available throughout the week!

Not all bacon is made equally, but you don't necessarily have to use the high-end slabs you can only find at a butcher shop. Just about anything will work, but some types are better for this recipe than others, and finding ways to use what you have is essential to tweaking it to your palate.

When it comes to center versus thick-cut bacon, you may be better off using something on the thinner side. Even turkey bacon is a solid choice, with similar protein and less fat, but only if it's easy to work with. Cooking times vary quite a bit depending on your method — this could take 10 to 15 minutes in the air fryer, or up to an hour and a half on the grill if you're cooking over low heat — but you only have two real goals for this recipe. The first is giving the bacon a nice, crispy texture. The second is bringing the meat to a safe level of doneness, following the package instructions for pork or turkey bacon.

If you're grilling, a toothpick or skewer is the best way to ensure your floppy bacon sticks to the onion ring, but your food can still be a bit delicate to move once it comes to room temperature. A quick trip to the fridge can help the meat stiffen enough to move onto the grill, where it should crisp and harden enough that it won't fall off quite so easily. This is also a good opportunity to let any additional seasoning soak into the meat, better infusing it with flavor.

#9659. The Egg McMuffin Hack A McDonald's Chef Loves

If you love starting your morning with a McDonald's Egg McMuffin, you aren't alone. The popular breakfast menu item is one of the most-ordered foods at the global burger chain, and perhaps part of its appeal is how versatile it is. As an example, you might order it cordon bleu-style for a heftier dose of protein, or follow the popular trend of adding a crunchy Hash Brown somewhere in between those English muffin halves. These are all well and good, but if you like a little sweetness with your savory, try the hack given to Food Republic by Wayne Kuhl, director of culinary for McDonald's: "Use the jellies, strawberry or grape jelly."

If you haven't ventured too far into the app beyond the sandwiches or the sides, you could have missed the Condiments section, and when you scroll nearly to the end, you'll find the Grape Jam and Strawberry Preserve of which Kuhl speaks. Spread onto the insides of a toasted English muffin, the bright fruit notes break up the heavy, salty bites of meat, egg, and melted cheese, striking that classic savory-sweet balance we're biologically hardwired to crave.

And Kuhl isn't alone in appreciating this creation. On Reddit, commenters shared their own love of this hack, with one person saying the McMuffin "just doesn't hit the same without the strawberry [jam]."

Just as a drizzle of hot honey elevates grilled cheese, turning it into a multidimensional feast, Wayne Kuhl's hack uses sweet jam to cut through the heavy, savory layers of the McMuffin. But there are actually quite a few options on McDonald's condiment menu if you don't go for fruity jelly.

You can also order packets of honey and drizzle that sweet nectar of the bees onto your McMuffin for a mild sweetness that might leave your hands a little sticky (totally worth it, though). Another sticky option is to pour on some of the syrup that more commonly accompanies the Big Breakfast. While it's not pure maple syrup, this addition nonetheless gives your breakfast sandwich a tasty new dimension, as the caramel-colored liquid at least mimics maple flavor.

Finally, you don't have to stick to typical breakfast condiments. McDonald's sauces are available all day, and there are some options that already blend the salty with the sweet, like the Sweet 'N Sour Dipping Sauce (which was semi-famously poured onto a McMuffin during a 1992 "SNL" skit). The Tangy Barbecue Sauce is another option that would taste great on the sandwich, as well as the Honey Mustard.

#9655. Grab This Tangy Ingredient For More Flavorful Fried Eggs (Hint: It's Not Hot Sauce Or Vinegar)

Fried eggs are one of the easiest, most filling breakfast foods you can prepare in a flash. While flavorful, they can also be a bit one-note, relying on fat and protein for much of their taste. That's why adding just a dash of pickle juice can completely transform them, cutting through that heartiness for something deliciously complex with next to no effort.

Pickles are a chemically complex ingredient that usually comes laden with both vinegar and salt, so there are a lot of ways to use leftover brine as an all-in-one seasoning and major kitchen helper. Similar to using vinegar for poached eggs, it's great at keeping egg whites firmly set and preventing them from feathering off into burnt little bits you need to scrape off later. Restaurant-quality fried eggs are easy to achieve by adding just a teaspoon of water and a lid, letting the bottoms crisp while the top whites and yolks reach tender perfection. But by substituting that water with brine, you're not only getting the same effect, but also easily and intensely seasoning the eggs.

This creates something tangy but creamy, rich but light. And if your brine came laden with herbs and other aromatics, it soaked up all those flavors, which you can now easily impart to your breakfast! Since you'll be adding it once your eggs have almost finished cooking, you won't even have to sacrifice the taste of your favorite butter or cooking fats.

Something as tangy, rich, and hearty as a fried egg has quite a bit of potential as a breakfast pairing. Since it's so easy to make, it's one of the simplest ways to upgrade other comfort dishes and introduce acid in a way that won't compromise their textures.

Restaurant-quality avocado toast doesn't skimp on the seasoning, usually incorporating some sort of acid, like lemon juice or vinegary hot sauce, to make it more complex. A fried egg is already a classic pairing, but one cooked in pickle juice easily provides the acid while letting you keep the fruit's texture to your preference, whether that's sliced, mashed, or creamy. A bit of acid plus a great egg can go a long way in many savory, hearty breakfast dishes, from steak and eggs to grits. Few accoutrements are quite as creamy, light, and tangy, and can brighten up even the heaviest foods.

Some breakfast dishes may need some lightening up but can't achieve the right texture if you add too much moisture. Something like hash browns or breakfast potatoes requires a dry environment to crisp up, and while some acid may improve their taste, it can come at the cost of their crispiness. A pickle juice fried egg layered on top not only adds creaminess from the yolk, but also helps cut through the heavier fats you used to prepare them for something a bit more comprehensively flavored, all without changing the recipe.

#9654. SkyW4lker Exposed: A Growing Microsoft 365 Phishing Threat to American Enterprises

Online interactive sandbox for DFIR/SOC investigations. Fast malware analysis and cybersecurity threat detection.

Online interactive sandbox for DFIR/SOC investigations. Fast malware analysis and cybersecurity threat detection.

Online interactive sandbox for DFIR/SOC investigations. Fast malware analysis and cybersecurity threat detection.

SkyW4lker (SkyW4lker x365 Sentinel) is an active device-code phishing kit targeting Microsoft 365 users in the United States, Europe, and other regions. By abusing Microsoft’s legitimate authentication process, the kit can give attackers access to corporate accounts without stealing passwords or bypassing MFA. This puts business emails, sensitive documents, and other Microsoft 365 resources at risk of unauthorized access.

The ANY.RUN team identified 618 sandbox analyses related to SkyW4lker between June and October 21, 2026, with 46% of submissions coming from the United States. Activity increased from 20 analyses in June to 200 in September, highlighting the growing exposure of organizations relying on Microsoft 365.

JavaScript obfuscation (obfuscator.io), Device-Code phishing, Geolocation detection, IP-address detection, CAPTCHA verification

Email attachments (.pdf, .docx, .xls/xlsx and others), redirection links and lure pages (including Google Maps, Google Images, Miro, Zoom and others)

URL patterns: /session_public.php?action= /endpoints/confirm_visit.php /js/url_helper.js /js/endpoint.js /js/client_geo.js

The United States accounts for 47% of SkyW4lker-related sandbox submissions, more than twice the share of any other country. With the campaign exploiting legitimate Microsoft authentication processes and routine business communications, these findings raise concerns for US enterprises about how effectively existing security controls can identify suspicious activity before it leads to account compromise.

SkyW4lker highlights several security risks that organizations need to account for when protecting business-critical systems and employee identities:

Stop account compromise before it disrupts your business.Detect threats earlier and reduce response costs.

You can examine the full SkyW4lker attack chain in this ANY.RUN Sandbox analysis.

The attacker sends the victim a phishing email with a password-protected attachment. Typical subjects involve commercial offers, contracts, invoices, or confidential documents. The attachment is a PDF, DOCX, or XLSX file, and the password is provided in the email body.

The document contains a link to a CAPTCHA page. Some variants include an additional lure page hosted on a legitimate service such as Miro, Google Sites, or Zoom, which redirects the victim to the next step.

Finally, the victim is directed to a phishing page that instructs them to enter a device code on Microsoft’s legitimate authentication page, potentially granting the attacker access to their Microsoft 365 account.

The phishing page relies on obfuscated JavaScript functions and separate script files. Using ANY.RUN’s In-Browser Data Inspection, analysts can examine the page’s DOM and HTTP activity to understand how these scripts operate.

The scripts keep the page in regular contact with the PHP backend and determine the location of the victim from their IP address. Within the page DOM, the main script loads additional modules, sets click handlers on buttons and builds GET requests to the PHP endpoint /session_public.php with the action parameter (start or poll).

With action=start, the script sends the geolocation and IP address of the victim and receives a session ID. After that, it sends a request with action=poll every few seconds to check whether the victim has authenticated.

The other modules of the phishing page are listed below:

Determines the location of the victim from the response of one of three services: ip-api[.]com, ipapi[.]co or ipwho[.]is. The location can also be obtained through the PHP endpoint php/endpoints/client_geo.php.

Base script with helper wrappers for URL handling, such as building GET parameters and appending slashes.

Tracks the state of the victim. It logs the e-mail address, password, browser, MFA status, country and other auxiliary fields used during authentication and sends them to the PHP backend at php/endpoints/accounts.php.
